content:
## Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) have achieved impressive results in complex reasoning and knowledge tasks, yet they often struggle with factual accuracy and logical consistency. Prior works have improved LLM performance using prompt-based techniques (e.g. chain-of-thought prompting and self-consistency) and post-hoc self-refinement, but these typically operate on a single model instance. Recently, multi-agent debate frameworks have emerged as a complementary approach, wherein multiple LLM agents propose answers and critique each other’s reasoning to reach consensus. Such a “society of minds” approach has been shown to significantly improve mathematical reasoning and reduce factual hallucinations. However, existing debate methods use homogeneous agents with simple majority voting, limiting their effectiveness. In this work, we propose Adaptive Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Debate (A-HMAD), a novel framework that extends multi-agent debate with (i) diverse specialized agents, (ii) dynamic debate routing, and (iii) a learned consensus mechanism. Each agent in A-HMAD is assigned a distinct role or expertise (e.g. logical reasoning, factual verification, strategic planning), enabling more comprehensive error-checking and perspective diversity than identical agents. A coordination policy dynamically selects which agents contribute at each round based on the question’s domain and the evolving debate state. To aggregate viewpoints, we introduce a consensus optimizer that learns to weight each agent’s vote according to its reliability and the confidence of its arguments. On six challenging benchmarks – including arithmetic QA, grade-school math (GSM8K), multifact question answering (MMLU), factual biography generation, and chess strategy – our A-HMAD consistently outperforms prior single-model methods and the original multi-agent debate baseline. Notably, A-HMAD achieves 4–6% absolute accuracy gains over standard debate on these tasks, and reduces factual errors by over 30% in biography facts. We provide extensive ablations demonstrating the benefits of agent heterogeneity, additional debate rounds, and the learned consensus module. Our findings suggest that an adaptive, role-diverse debating ensemble can drive significant advances in LLM-based educational reasoning, paving the way for safer, more interpretable, and pedagogically reliable AI systems.

### Similar content being viewed by others

## 1 Introduction

Large-scale pre-trained language models have revolutionized NLP, demonstrating remarkable prowess in tasks requiring knowledge and reasoning (Brown et al. 2020; Srivastava et al. 2023). Models like GPT-3 and its successors exhibit strong few-shot learning abilities (Brown et al. 2020) and can generate coherent multi-step reasoning chains when prompted appropriately (Kojima et al. 2022). Despite these gains, even state-of-the-art LLMs often produce hallucinations – confidently stated false facts – and illogical reasoning leaps, undermining their reliability (Lin et al. 2021; Ji et al. 2023). This is due in part to the noisy, unverified nature of web-scale training data and the lack of explicit reasoning verification in standard next-token prediction training (Ouyang et al. 2022; Ziegler et al. 2019). Improving the factual accuracy and reasoning soundness of LLM outputs has therefore become a pressing research goal (Lee et al. 2022; Kadavath et al. 2022).

A rich body of recent work has explored techniques to mitigate LLM reasoning and factual errors. Prompting strategies such as providing step-by-step exemplars or eliciting a chain-of-thought (CoT) have led to notable improvements in arithmetic and commonsense reasoning (Kojima et al. 2022; Wei et al. 2022). For example, Wei et al. (2022) showed that CoT prompting enables models to break down problems into logical steps, and Kojima et al. (2022) found that even zero-shot prompts (e.g. “Let’s think step by step”) can induce multi-step reasoning in LLMs. Building on CoT, self-consistency decoding samples multiple reasoning paths and selects the most common answer, which boosts correctness by averaging out reasoning variance (Wang et al. 2022). Other works equip LLMs with scratchpads or external tools: Nye et al. (2021) introduced “scratchpad” memory for intermediate computations, and tool-use approaches allow models to consult calculators or knowledge bases to check facts (Yao et al. 2023; Schick et al. 2023). Orthogonal to prompting, learning-from-feedback methods like reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) fine-tune models to favor truthful, helpful outputs (Christiano et al. 2017; Stiennon et al. 2020), significantly reducing toxic or untrue generations (Siddiky et al. 2025). Likewise, post-hoc verifier models have been trained to check and correct a model’s answers (e.g. for math word problems Cobbe et al., 2021). Another promising direction is self-reflection and refinement, where the model iteratively critiques and improves its own output (Kawamura et al. 2003; Madaan et al. 2023). Madaan et al. (2023) showed that prompting an LLM to reflect on potential errors and then attempt a revised solution can yield more accurate results, echoing human problem-solving strategies (Renze and Guven 2024). Despite these advances, most techniques above involve a single model reasoning in isolation; the model may still overlook certain errors or fail to verify all facts due to its inherent biases or blind spots (Kadavath et al. 2022; Wei et al. 2022).

In contrast to single-model approaches, multi-agent frameworks draw inspiration from social or argumentative processes in which multiple experts collaborate or debate to reach a better answer (Michael et al. 2023). Early conceptual work by Minsky (Michael et al. 2023) posited that intelligent behavior could emerge from a “Society of Mind” – a diverse collection of simpler agents. In the context of AI alignment and truthfulness, Khan et al. (2024) proposed AI debate, where two agents argue for opposing answers and a judge (human or AI) decides which argument is more convincing. The hope is that through adversarial debate, the truth would prevail because any false argument can be revealed by the opponent (Khan et al. 2024). While Irving’s work was theoretical, recent empirical studies have started to realize the benefits of multi-agent interactions. For example, Li et al. (2023) introduced a communicative multi-agent system (Camel) where agents with different roles (user, assistant, critic) collaborate to solve tasks. Similarly, MetaGPT by Hong et al. (2023) uses multiple specialized agent personas (e.g. PM, engineer, tester) to decompose and solve complex programming tasks, showing the power of role specialization. Focusing on language tasks, Kadavath et al. (2022) demonstrated that allowing two LLMs to debate from different viewpoints encourages divergent thinking and can improve answer quality. Parrish et al. (2022) found that when a less truthful LLM “debates” a more truthful LLM, the resulting answers tend to be more factual, suggesting that persuasion by a knowledgeable agent can correct the other’s misconceptions. These works hint that multi-agent interaction might overcome individual model limitations. However, some studies report mixed results; Chan et al. (2023) showed that a simple two-turn debate did not significantly help humans answer reading comprehension questions, implying that how debate is structured is critical.

Most relevant to our work, Du et al. (2023) recently proposed a multiagent debate framework for LLMs to improve both reasoning and factuality. In their approach, multiple instances of the same LLM are each prompted to generate an answer with reasoning. The agents then exchange their answers and critique each other’s reasoning over several rounds, before outputting a final consensus answer (Du et al. 2023). This method, requiring only black-box access to the models’ outputs, was shown to significantly enhance performance on math word problems, strategic games, and factual QA, compared to single-agent baselines (Du et al. 2023). Notably, Du et al. reported that debate reduces hallucinations: agents often identify and remove one another’s uncertain or inconsistent facts, leading to a final answer with more reliable information (Du et al. 2023; Kadavath et al. 2022). The multiagent debate can be seen as inducing an ensemble-like effect where multiple reasoning paths are explored in parallel and vetted against each other, yielding higher confidence when they converge (Du et al. 2023; Kadavath et al. 2022). Zhang et al. (2023) further applied a debating agents idea for LLM-based evaluation, showing that a multi-agent debate can refine judgment of answers. Wu et al. (2024) used debates between a “student” and “professor” model to supervise and improve unreliable reasoning, while Zelikman et al. (2022) leveraged cooperative agents for embodied decision-making. These underline a growing consensus that multi-agent interactions can enhance an LLM’s performance and reliability.

Despite the promise of multi-agent debate, there remain clear opportunities for improvement. First, prior debate frameworks largely use homogeneous agents – e.g. identical GPT-3.5 models with the same prompting style (Du et al. 2023). This limits the diversity of perspectives; if all agents share similar strengths and weaknesses, certain errors may go unchallenged. Recent works in multi-agent collaboration emphasize heterogeneity as a key factor for success (Li et al. 2023; Hong et al. 2023), which suggests that introducing specialized agents could further improve the debate outcome. Second, existing methods rely on a simple majority vote or unanimous agreement for the final answer (Du et al. 2023; Kadavath et al. 2022). This treats all agents as equally reliable, ignoring the possibility that some agents (or certain argument lines) might be more likely correct than others. A more nuanced consensus mechanism that weights agents by their past accuracy or the confidence of their justifications could lead to more robust final answers. Third, the debate protocol in prior work is static – agents alternate in a fixed order and number of rounds (Du et al. 2023). In complex scenarios, a rigid protocol might be suboptimal: for example, if a particular agent has expertise most relevant to the query, the framework should allocate more opportunity for that agent to contribute. Conversely, irrelevant or redundant agents could be bypassed to save computation. Such dynamic agent routing or adaptive scheduling of debate rounds has not been explored in existing work. Finally, no prior study (to our knowledge) has integrated an explicit learning component into the debate loop – the interplay is handled by prompting alone. This raises the question of whether parts of the multi-agent debate process (e.g. how to aggregate answers) can be learned from data to further boost performance.

In this paper, we propose a new framework called Adaptive Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Debate (A-HMAD) that addresses the above limitations and substantially improves LLM factuality and reasoning via multi-agent debate. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

-
1.
We design a heterogeneous agent ensemble where each agent has a specialized role or distinct model type. By incorporating diverse reasoning skills (e.g. a “Verifier” agent focused on fact-checking and a “Solver” agent focused on computation), our debate encourages complementary critiques that were absent in prior homogeneous debates. We also introduce a dynamic routing strategy that activates different subsets of agents depending on the query type and intermediate debate outcomes, thereby allocating expertise where needed and reducing redundancy.

-
2.
We propose a learned consensus module that replaces simple majority voting for final answer selection. This module uses features of each agent’s responses and confidence (such as consistency of an agent’s answers across rounds) to weight their contributions when synthesizing the final answer. We train the consensus optimizer on a corpus of debate transcripts with known ground-truth answers, using a loss that rewards choosing the correct answer. To our knowledge, this is the first learning-based aggregation method in an LLM debate framework. It yields more accurate final decisions, especially in cases where a minority agent is actually correct and should override a noisy majority.

-
3.
We thoroughly evaluate A-HMAD on the six challenging benchmarks. Our method achieves new state-of-the-art results on all tasks for the base model used (Llama-2 70B-chat in our experiments), outperforming the original multi-agent debate by 4–6 percentage points in accuracy across the board. For instance, on GSM8K, A-HMAD scores 90.2% versus 84.0% by standard debate and 77.0% by a single CoT model. On a factual biography dataset, A-HMAD cuts the rate of incorrect facts per biography by 45% relative to single-agent outputs. We also compare to other baselines including zero-shot CoT, self-reflection, self-consistency ensemble, and a recent multi-agent divergent-thinking method, finding that our approach surpasses all of them significantly.

-
4.
Through controlled ablations, we quantify the impact of each component of A-HMAD. We show that heterogeneity contributes a considerable boost (e.g. replacing specialized agents with identical ones drops performance by up to 3.5% on reasoning tasks), and the learned consensus yields more correct final answers in cases of agent disagreement (improving final accuracy by 5% when initial agent votes are split). We analyze how performance scales with the number of debate rounds and agents, confirming that our adaptive strategy can effectively leverage additional agents better than a static debate. Qualitatively, we present case studies illustrating how an expert agent can correct others (e.g. the fact-checker agent catching a historical date error that all other agents believed, thereby steering the group to a truthful answer). These insights illuminate why A-HMAD succeeds and provide guidance for future multi-LLM systems.


In summary, our work advances the state-of-the-art in LLM reasoning and factual accuracy by marrying the strengths of multi-agent debate with architectural and algorithmic innovations. By allowing a set of diverse LLMs to “think together” and learn how to optimally integrate their knowledge, A-HMAD moves closer to the vision of robust, truth-seeking AI systems that can reliably solve complex problems and self-correct errors. We release our code and model configurations to facilitate further research in this direction.

## 2 Related work

### 2.1 Large language models and reasoning

The emergence of large pre-trained language models (LLMs) has led to unprecedented performance on a range of NLP tasks (Brown et al. 2020; Srivastava et al. 2023). Beyond standard tasks, researchers have probed LLMs’ ability to perform multi-step reasoning. Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting (Wei et al. 2022) was a breakthrough technique: by prompting models to generate intermediate reasoning steps (e.g. “First, let’s calculate X...”), it significantly improved arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks. Wei et al. (2022) showed that even models with tens of billions of parameters, like PaLM 62B, benefited from CoT, nearly doubling their solve rate on some math problems compared to direct answers. Subsequent work by Kojima et al. (2022) revealed that even without few-shot examples, simply appending a phrase like “Let’s think step by step” often elicits CoT reasoning from LLMs (a phenomenon termed zero-shot CoT).

Building on CoT, self-consistency decoding (SC) was proposed by Wang et al. (2022). Instead of taking the first answer from a chain-of-thought prompt, SC samples multiple reasoning paths and then selects the most frequent answer among them. This approach leverages the intuition that independent reasoning samples that converge on the same answer are likely correct. Indeed, self-consistency improved accuracy on arithmetic and commonsense QA benchmarks by 2–5% over standard CoT (Wang et al. 2022). Subsequent variants have explored ranking or filtering generated reasoning chains by likelihood or other heuristics (Chen et al. 2023).

Another line of research incorporates intermediate computation or tool use. For example, scratchpad methods (Nye et al. 2021) allow the model to generate and reuse intermediate variables or notes (often by fine-tuning on chain-of-thought data), which was shown to help models systematically work through math problems. LLMs augmented with external tools take this further: they can call APIs such as calculators, web search engines, or knowledge retrieval systems as part of their reasoning process (Yao et al. 2023; Schick et al. 2023). Prominent examples include the ReAct framework by Yao et al. (2023), where an LLM interleaves reasoning with actions (like API calls) to fetch information, and Schick et al. (2023), which augments a model’s training data with demonstrations of tool use. These methods can dramatically improve factual accuracy for things like arithmetic or open-domain QA, as the model can offload certain tasks to reliable tools.

### 2.2 Addressing hallucinations and factual accuracy

LLM hallucination (generating false or unfounded statements) has been widely recognized and a number of strategies aim to mitigate it. Retrieval-augmented generation is one approach: e.g. REALM (Guu et al. 2020) and RAG (Lewis et al. 2020) integrate a differentiable retrieval component so that the language model can condition on relevant documents from a knowledge base, leading to more factually grounded output. Another approach is post-hoc verification – using a separate model or module to fact-check the LLM’s outputs. Cobbe et al. (2021) trained verifiers for math word problems that check a proposed solution and predict correctness, boosting reliability when used to rerank answers. For truth-oriented QA, Lin et al. introduced TruthfulQA, a benchmark and analysis of LLM truthfulness Lin et al. (2021), and found that even large models frequently output “plausible falsehoods”. To combat this, Lee et al. (2022) proposed fine-tuning LMs on cleaned “truthful” data and using calibrated generation methods, which yielded Factuality Enhanced LMs with reduced hallucination rates. Another direction has been calibration and uncertainty estimation: Achiam et al. (2023) showed that LLMs do have some internal awareness of when they don’t know (their predicted probabilities correlate with correctness), suggesting that prompting or training methods that extract this self-knowledge could help avoid incorrect answers.

Inspired by human self-monitoring, researchers have equipped LLMs with the ability to reflect on and correct their own outputs. The Reflexion framework by Kawamura et al. (2003) demonstrated that an agent which stores memory of past mistakes and self-corrective feedback can solve decision-making tasks more reliably. In the context of question-answering and reasoning, various prompt-based methods have the model critique its initial solution and then try again. For instance, Madaan et al. (2023) introduced Self-Refine, where the model generates an initial answer, then is prompted to identify errors or areas of improvement, and produces a refined answer iteratively. This method improved performance on tasks like code generation and story writing. Similarly, in a “reflective” CoT, the model might produce a reasoning path, then verify each step for consistency or errors (Renze and Guven 2024). Renze and Guven (2024) conducted a study with eight types of self-reflection prompts and found that across multiple domains (math, science, etc.), self-reflection allowed models like GPT-4 and LLaMA to significantly improve their problem-solving success rates. These approaches all leverage multiple passes of reasoning – either explicitly or implicitly – to catch mistakes that a single-pass generation would miss (Kadavath et al. 2022; Hendrycks et al. 2021).

### 2.3 Multi-agent and debate approaches

Multi-agent systems have a rich history in AI, but only recently have they been applied to large language models for complex reasoning. Debate as an AI paradigm was first articulated by Khan et al. (2024), who argued that two AIs debating could allow a human judge to accurately determine the truth of an answer, even if the judge cannot directly solve the problem, by evaluating the debaters’ arguments. Following this idea, several works have attempted to implement debating LMs. Kadavath et al. (2022) presented a simple two-agent debate where each agent gives an answer and then they exchange critiques; this was shown to increase answer diversity and sometimes quality, as each agent might bring up points the other missed. Du et al. (2023); Minsky (1986) extended this to multi-agent (more than two) and multi-round debates, finding strong quantitative gains on reasoning benchmarks. In their Multiagent Debate framework, three agents debated over two rounds and reached a final answer by consensus, outperforming single-agent chain-of-thought by 5–10% absolute on tasks like GSM8K math and MMLU knowledge questions (Du et al. 2023). Interestingly, Du et al. also created a new evaluation of factual consistency (biography generation) and showed debate greatly reduced errors such as misstated affiliations or dates (Du et al. 2023).

Other contemporaneous works have enriched the debate paradigm. Parrish et al. (2022) specifically examined debates where one agent is more persuasive or higher-quality than the other, and showed that less truthful models can be guided towards truth by the influence of a more truthful model during debate. Their experiments with GPT-4 “coaching” weaker GPT-3.5 models resulted in the latter producing fewer false answers (Parrish et al. 2022). Zhang et al. (2023) introduced ChatEval, a framework that uses multi-agent debates to evaluate candidate answers: multiple AI critics discuss which answer is better, aiming to produce more reliable evaluations than a single evaluator. Wu et al. (2024) leveraged debate in a training setup: a “professor” model poses questions and critiques a “student” model’s answers, and the student is updated based on the feedback. They found this debate-based supervision improved the student’s performance on tricky questions. In multi-agent collaboration (as opposed to adversarial debate), Li et al. (Camel) (Li et al. 2023) showed that role-playing two chat agents (e.g. as a user and assistant) with iterative feedback can produce better solutions for tasks like code and story generation. Wu et al. (AutoGen) (Thoppilan et al. 2022) proposed a general multi-agent conversational framework where agents (which could be LLMs or tools) communicate to solve user requests, demonstrating complex interactions such as one agent decomposing a task and another executing subtasks. Our work is aligned with these trends but distinct in explicitly focusing on heterogeneous debate with more than two agents and introducing learnable mechanisms into the debate.

The idea of combining multiple model outputs to improve reliability has parallels in classical ensemble learning. Techniques like majority voting, weighted voting, or stacking have long been used to boost accuracy by aggregating diverse models (Dietterich 2000). In LLM context, self-consistency (Wang et al. 2022) can be seen as an ensemble of reasoning paths from one model. Multi-agent debate takes this further by enabling interaction between the “ensemble members” before the final aggregation (Du et al. 2023; Kadavath et al. 2022). There is also a connection to consensus methods in generative modeling: Li et al. (2022) introduced an iterative consensus approach for combining outputs of different pretrained models (like vision or language models) by having them communicate and converge. While their setting was multimodal and not adversarial, the notion of reaching consensus via communication is shared. Our consensus optimizer extends ideas from weighted ensembling and learns how to best combine agents’ answers. Additionally, our dynamic agent routing draws inspiration from mixture-of-experts models (Sabour et al. 2017), where different neural experts handle different inputs; in our case, we manually define expert agents and route queries to them selectively, akin to a human delegating questions to domain specialists.

In summary, our work synthesizes ideas from prompting-based reasoning enhancement, debate frameworks, and ensemble consensus. To the best of our knowledge, A-HMAD is the first to incorporate agent heterogeneity, adaptive interaction, and learned aggregation all in one multi-agent LLM system. By comparing to representative methods from each category (CoT, reflection, voting, prior debate) in our experiments, we position A-HMAD at the intersection and demonstrate its advantages over each individual line of work.

## 3 Methodology

In this section, we formalize the task setting and describe the architecture of Adaptive Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Debate (A-HMAD) (Fig. 1). We begin with an overview of the problem and a recap of the standard multi-agent debate procedure for context. We then present our enhancements: diverse agent roles, the adaptive debate protocol, and the consensus optimization module. Throughout, we use mathematical notation to precisely define the behavior of the agents and the learning objectives.

### 3.1 Problem formulation

We consider a general question-answering task with reasoning, formalized as follows. Let *x* denote an input query (e.g. a math word problem or a knowledge question), and let *y* be the correct answer from some answer space \( \mathcal {Y}\). For open-ended generation tasks like writing a factual biography, *y* would be a correct text passage; for classification or short-answer tasks, *y* might be a discrete label or numeric result. An LLM with parameters \(\theta \) defines a conditional probability \(P_\theta (y, r \mid x)\) over answer *y* and a reasoning trace *r* (the sequence of tokens comprising its chain-of-thought reasoning). During inference, standard decoding seeks the most likely or highest-scoring output according to \(P_\theta \). In few-shot or CoT prompting, \(P_\theta \) is influenced by additional prompt context but still uses one model’s knowledge.

The goal is to maximize the accuracy \(\Pr (\hat{y} = y^*)\) of the final predicted answer \(\hat{y}\) compared to the ground truth \(y^*\), while minimizing any factual errors or invalid reasoning in the output. We assume access to *N* instances of potentially different LLMs, which we label as agents \(A_1, A_2, \dots , A_N\). Each agent \(A_i\) can be viewed as an oracle that, given a prompt (which may include the question and some dialogue context), outputs an answer and reasoning. Formally, agent \(A_i\) with parameters \(\theta _i\) induces a distribution \(P_{\theta _i}(y, r \mid \text {prompt})\). We treat each agent as a black box generator: we do not fine-tune these agents on the specific tasks, although later we introduce a small trainable module outside the agents.

A debate protocol orchestrates interactions among these agents to produce a final answer. Let *R* be the number of debate rounds. In each round \(r = 0, 1, \dots , R\), each agent may produce a message. A message typically consists of an answer candidate and an accompanying rationale or critique. We denote by \(a_{i}^{(r)}\) the answer proposed by agent *i* at the end of round *r*, and by \(r_{i}^{(r)}\) its reasoning in that round. The collection of all agents’ outputs in round *r* is denoted \(S^{(r)} = {(a_{1}^{(r)}, r_{1}^{(r)}), \dots , (a_{N}^{(r)}, r_{N}^{(r)})}\). The debate begins with each agent independently answering the question:

-
**Round 0 (Initialization)**: For each \(i \in {1,\dots ,N}\), agent \(A_i\) receives the query*x*and produces an initial answer \(a_i^{(0)}\) with reasoning \(r_i^{(0)}\). This can be thought of as each agent’s solo solution to the problem. No interaction has occurred yet. Mathematically, \(a_i^{(0)}, r_i^{(0)} \sim P_{\theta _i}(y, r \mid x, p_i^{(0)})\), where \(p_i^{(0)}\) is the initial prompt given to agent*i*(which may include instructions specific to that agent’s role, as we introduce later).

After the initial round, the debate proceeds with interaction. In each subsequent round, agents see (some of) the other agents’ prior answers and provide updated answers:

-
Round

*r*(Debate step): For \(r = 1\) to*R*, each agent \(A_i\) is prompted with the query*x*plus a transcript of previous rounds’ communications (e.g. the answers or arguments from other agents in round \(r-1\)). Based on this information, agent*i*outputs a revised answer \(a_i^{(r)}\) along with any new reasoning \(r_i^{(r)}\). This can be formalized as:$$\begin{aligned} a_{i}^{(r)},r_{i}^{(r)}\sim P_{\theta _{i}}\left( y,r|x,\underbrace{(a_{1}^{(r-1)},r_{1}^{(r-1)}),\ldots ,(a_{N}^{(r-1)},r_{N}^{(r-1)})}_{\text {transcript of round }r-1},p_{i}^{(r)}\right) , \end{aligned}$$(1)where \(p_i^{(r)}\) is the prompt template for agent

*i*at round*r*. In essence, agent*i*“reads” the others’ round \((r-1)\) responses and possibly its own previous answer, then produces a new answer. Agents can agree or disagree with others, point out mistakes, or correct their own answer based on the discussion.

The debate ends after *R* rounds, yielding final answer proposals \(a_1^{(R)}, \dots , a_N^{(R)}\) from each agent. The system must then derive a single consensus answer \(\hat{y}\) from these. In prior work, the consensus is typically the answer that the majority of agents gave in the final round (or if all agents converged, that unanimous answer). Formally, one could write:

where \(\mathbb {I}{\cdot }\) is the indicator function. \(\hat{y}_{\text {maj}}\) is simply the most common final answer. If no answer is majority (e.g. a tie among *N* answers), one could break ties arbitrarily or by some confidence heuristic; in practice, with an odd number of agents or enough debate rounds, tie situations are rare.

The key empirical finding of multi-agent debate is that under a well-crafted protocol (with appropriate prompt instructions), the agents often converge to the same answer (\(a_1^{(R)} = a_2^{(R)} = \cdots = a_N^{(R)}\)) and that answer is more likely to be correct than any individual’s initial answer. Debate thus serves to cross-verify reasoning: agents correct each other’s errors and reinforce correct partial solutions.

However, as outlined earlier, the standard debate has shortcomings: all agents are identical (\(\theta _1=\theta _2=\cdots \)) and use the same prompting strategy \(p_i^{(r)}\), and the consensus mechanism is a simple vote. We next describe how A-HMAD improves upon this baseline.

### 3.2 Multi-agent debate baseline recap

Before detailing our approach, we provide pseudocode for the baseline multi-agent debate to make the subsequent extensions clearer. Algorithm 1 summarizes the procedure for *N* agents and *R* rounds.

In Round 0, all agents independently answer the question. In each subsequent round, each agent sees what others answered previously and then produces a new answer. The final answer is chosen by majority vote. This baseline assumes all agents \(A_i\) are the same underlying model (e.g. multiple copies of GPT-3.5) with the same prompting format. It also assumes every agent participates in every round.

### 3.3 Proposed heterogeneous agent roles

In A-HMAD, we depart from homogeneity by assigning distinct roles or model types to agents. The intuition is that different agents can excel at different aspects of the task, making the debate more effective at catching errors. We define a set of roles \( {R_1, R_2, \dots , R_K}\) that our agents will cover. Each agent \(A_i\) is associated with one role \(R_{k(i)}\). Roles could be implemented in two (complementary) ways:

-
Specialized Prompting: Agents share the same base model architecture but are given different role instructions in their prompt. For example, one agent might be prompted “You are a rigorous mathematician who double-checks calculations”, while another is prompted “You are a fact-checker with access to reliable knowledge”. These differing personas bias the agents’ behavior. Prior work suggests that even with identical base LLMs, role prompts can induce significantly different responses. We leverage this to create virtual specialists.

-
Different Model Backbones: We can also choose agents to be different pretrained models entirely. For instance, one agent could be GPT-4 (stronger at logical reasoning), and another could be a domain-specific model (e.g. a chess engine or a smaller model fine-tuned on math). In our experiments, we primarily use the same model class for a fair comparison, but we also demonstrate a hybrid setting (mixing GPT-4 and ChatGPT) to show the benefit of a stronger model guiding weaker ones.


Without loss of generality, assume we have *N* agents and *K* distinct roles, where \(K \le N\). Let \(\mathcal {I}_k = { i \mid A_i \text { has role } R_k }\) be the set of agent indices for each role. Each role \(R_k\) comes with a specific prompt prefix and behavioral guidelines. For example, we use the following roles in our implementation:

-
**Solver**: Focuses on solving the problem step-by-step. Prompt emphasizes logical progression and correctness of calculations. -
**Checker**: Focuses on verifying others’ answers. Prompt instructs to be skeptical and find flaws or inconsistencies in any provided solution. -
**Knowledge Guru**: Specialized in factual recall. Prompt suggests the agent should provide relevant factual information or counterexamples if it suspects a factual error. -
**Conciliator**: (Optional) A role that tries to reconcile different answers and push the group towards consensus, possibly summarizing arguments.

Each agent’s generation in the debate now conditions not only on the debate context but also on its role instruction. The generation equation becomes:

In Round 0, the initial prompt for agent *i* would include its role description. For example:

*Agent i (Role = Checker) initial prompt:*

* "You are a *Checker* agent. Your job is to critique answers and find any mistakes.* * Question:* \(<x>\)

* Give your answer and reasoning. If unsure, explain what needs checking."*

Whereas a Solver’s prompt might encourage a direct solving approach:

*Agent j (Role = Solver) initial prompt: "You are a *Solver* agent. Solve the question step by step and give the answer at the end."*

This way, \(a_i^{(0)}\) from a Checker might actually be a partial answer or even a statement of uncertainty, but combined with identification of what needs verification – e.g., “Agent i: I suspect the answer is 42, but I need to double-check the calculation of the second step.” Meanwhile the Solver might confidently assert an answer. These differing perspectives set the stage for a richer debate in Round 1.

To make the role-specific behaviors reproducible, we explicitly designed separate prompt templates for each agent. The Solver focuses on step-by-step logical derivation and may optionally call a calculator API for numeric verification (though all main experiments were run without external tool use for fair comparison). The Checker critically inspects other agents’ reasoning and flags inconsistencies or arithmetic slips. The Knowledge Guru emphasizes factual correctness; it can query a retrieval module for verifying entity-based facts (e.g., dates, affiliations) when the task type is factual QA or biography generation. The Conciliator summarizes major points of agreement and disagreement to facilitate convergence in later rounds. We provide the full prompt templates for all roles, including any tool-use configurations, in Figs. 2, 3, 4, 5 for reproducibility.

Crucially, heterogeneity increases the chance that if one agent is wrong, another catches the error. For instance, on a math problem, a Solver might make a calculation error, but the Checker role is explicitly seeking such errors and will call it out in the next round. A Knowledge Guru might inject a forgotten fact (e.g., a historical date) that others didn’t recall. Formally, we expect that for any given mistake in reasoning or fact, \(\exists k\) such that an agent with role \(R_k\) is likely to notice and correct it. While this is hard to guarantee theoretically, it is supported by empirical results.

We typically maintain at most one agent per role in our experiments (\(N=K\)), except possibly duplicating a role if we want multiple independent agents with the same specialization. Redundant agents with the same role can increase the diversity of thought even within that specialty, akin to having two mathematicians solve the problem independently.

### 3.4 Dynamic agent participation

Standard debate uses all agents in every round (Algorithm 1). We introduce a dynamic routing mechanism that can modulate which agents are active in each round based on the state of the debate. This is motivated by efficiency (why involve agents unnecessarily if the debate is converging?) and accuracy (focus on the agents most likely to contribute at a given point).

We implement dynamic participation with a simple policy: at each round, an agent may be skipped (not prompted) if the system predicts its contribution would be redundant or less useful. Conversely, the policy might decide to invoke an additional round with certain agents if the debate hasn’t reached a confident consensus. Our policy uses two heuristics:

-
**Relevance-based activation**: We define a function \(\rho (i, x)\) that estimates the relevance of agent*i*’s role to question*x*. For example, if*x*is a pure math problem, \(\rho (\text {KnowledgeGuru}, x)\) might be low since factual recall is not needed; a chess question would have high \(\rho \) for a “ChessExpert” agent (if we had such a role). We implement \(\rho \) by simple keyword matching and task type detection (details in Experiments). At round 0, we only activate agents whose \(\rho (i,x)\) is above a threshold. Thus, some agents might not even give an initial answer if they are deemed irrelevant to the query. This prevents, say, a Knowledge agent from distracting the debate on a arithmetic problem. Disagreement-based activation: Let \(d^{(r)}\) be a measure of disagreement among agents’ answers in round*r*. One simple measure is the entropy of the answer distribution among agents:$$\begin{aligned} d^{(r)}=-\sum _{y\in \mathcal {Y}}P^{(r)}(y)\log P^{(r)}(y), \end{aligned}$$(4)where \(P^{(r)}(y) = \frac{1}{N}\sum _{i=1}^N \mathbb {I}{a_i^{(r)} = y}\) is the fraction of agents with answer

*y*in that round. \(d^{(r)} = 0\) means full agreement, and it increases as opinions diverge. If \(d^{(r-1)}\) is high (e.g. agents are split 2 vs 1 on different answers after round \(r-1\)), our policy will continue the debate to round*r*as usual. If \(d^{(r-1)}\) is low (consensus emerging), we can consider dropping some agents whose answers consistently align with others, to reduce redundancy. Specifically, if an agent \(A_i\) has given the same answer as another agent for two consecutive rounds and has not contributed any unique critique, we might skip prompting \(A_i\) in the next round and assume it would agree. This is an aggressive optimization that we apply only if needed for efficiency in large*N*settings. -
Expert intervention: If a minority agent holds a different answer from the majority and \(d^{(r-1)}\) is moderate, we can bring in a specialized agent (if available) for one round to resolve the dispute. For example, imagine 4 agents, and in round 1 three answer “A” while one agent (the Checker) says “I disagree, the answer should be B because of X”. We might deploy an external Tool or a high-precision agent (like GPT-4 if our main agents are weaker) in round 2 to double-check the point

*X*raised. This is like calling an expert witness in a debate. We include an instance of this in a case study for factual disputes, where we let a retrieval-augmented agent quickly fact-check a claim. Formally, we temporarily extend the agent set \(A_1,\dots ,A_N\) with a special agent \(A_{N+1}\) for round*r*, where \(A_{N+1}\) is configured for the specific dispute (e.g. query a knowledge base). After it provides input, it may be removed or remain inactive in other rounds.

The above can be encoded in a scheduling algorithm. Algorithm 2 outlines the dynamic debate controller. Note that dynamic control does not change the fundamental round-based structure; it only decides which agents produce outputs in a given round and when to stop the debate.

Key functions include \(should_{skip(i, r)}\) which checks if agent *i*’s answer has been redundant, and \({compose}_{prompt}\) which builds the round-specific prompt with only active agents’ transcripts. This algorithm yields a (possibly reduced) set of final answers at the last round \(R_f\).

After obtaining final answers (which may be fewer than *N* if some were skipped or if some converged and were not explicitly prompted), we pass them to the consensus module.

Dynamic scheduling ensures that each agent plays to its strengths and that the debate terminates as soon as a high-confidence consensus is formed. In practice, we cap \(R_{\text {max}}\) to 3 or 4 to limit cost, as we found most disagreements resolve by then for our tasks. If \(R_{\text {max}}\) is reached and there is still significant disagreement, we take it as a signal that the question is hard or ambiguous; in that case, our system can either output the top answer with a disclaimer or escalate (not explored here).

-
The number of agents supporting answer

*y*(i.e. majority voting influence). -
The confidence or authority of agents supporting

*y*. For instance, if a certain agent \(A_k\) historically has high accuracy on similar questions, its vote might be given more weight. We implement this by learning per-role or per-agent weights. -
Signals from the content of reasoning \(r_i^{(R)}\). If agent

*i*gave answer*y*, but its justification is shaky or self-contradictory, perhaps that vote should count less. Conversely, a very detailed and sound reasoning in support of*y*could boost \(s_y\).

One simple parameterization we use is:

where \(w_{k(i)}\) is a learned weight for the role of agent *i* (shared across agents of same role, if multiple), and \(\text {Conf}(r_i)\) is a numeric confidence estimate extracted from agent *i*’s reasoning content. We derive \(\text {Conf}(r_i)\) by a separate small classifier on the agent’s textual answer that looks for certain keywords or uncertainty markers, or by the model’s own probability of the answer if available. The coefficient \(\beta \) is a hyperparameter or learned scaling. Essentially, \(w_{k}\) tells how trustworthy role \(R_k\)’s answers are on average, and the second term adjusts for the specific answer’s perceived confidence. If an agent says “I’m 100% sure the answer is 42 because ...”, that might yield a higher \(\text {Conf}\) score versus an agent saying “I guess the answer is 42”.

For clarity, the confidence term \(\text {Conf}(r_i)\) is produced by a lightweight logistic classifier trained to estimate the internal consistency and assertiveness of each agent’s justification. We extract features such as the presence of hedging or uncertainty expressions (e.g., “maybe,” “probably”), self-assurance cues (e.g., “I am certain,” “definitely”), and the normalized log-probability of the predicted answer token if available. These features are aggregated through a sigmoid layer to yield a confidence score between 0 and 1.

The consensus module is trained on 200 synthetic debate transcripts generated from a separate pool of prompts that are fully disjoint from all evaluation benchmarks (Arithmetic, GSM8K, MMLU, etc.), ensuring no data leakage. We optimize the module using a cross-entropy loss between the predicted consensus distribution and the ground-truth correctness label. For instances where no agent provides the correct answer (“missed instances”), we apply a small uniform penalty to all candidate scores (i.e., \(\Delta s_y = -\epsilon \), \(\epsilon = 0.05\)), preventing overconfidence and stabilizing training under sparse supervision.

We train \(f_{\phi }\) in a supervised manner on a validation set of debates (which can be generated using our agents on a set of questions with known answers). For each debate instance, we have the final round agent answers \({a_i^{(R)}}\) and the ground truth \(y^*\). We define a loss that penalizes choosing an answer other than \(y^*\). For example, a cross-entropy loss can be used if we treat \(s_y\) as logits:

Since in many cases \(\mathcal {Y}\) might be large or continuous (e.g. open text), we simplify by only considering the answers actually proposed by agents (plus possibly an “other” option). In training, if none of the agents proposed the correct answer (which occasionally happens), we treat it as a missed instance or provide a small gradient nudging all \(s_y\) down (since none are correct). We found that even a modest dataset of 200 debate outcomes was enough to learn useful weights \({w_k}\). The learned weights reflected intuitive patterns – e.g. the “Checker” role was assigned a high positive weight (its dissent is often correct), whereas a generic “Solver” role had a lower weight (since it sometimes sticks to an incorrect solution). This suggests \(f_{\phi }\) successfully captured differing reliability. We also allowed a bias term for having more votes: effectively the module learned that two agents saying answer *A* is usually better than one agent saying *B*, all else equal.

At test time, the consensus module takes the final outputs of the debate and computes scores. We then output \(\hat{y}{\text {A-HMAD}} = \arg \max _y s_y\). If \(f{\phi }\) is linear as above, this is trivial to compute. In cases of perfect agreement (\(a_1^{(R)} = \cdots = a_N^{(R)}\)), \(s_y\) will obviously be highest for that unanimous *y* and we output it (similar to baseline). The benefit comes in cases of disagreement: e.g., if 2 agents say “1975” and 1 agent (the Knowledge Guru) says “1976” for a birthdate question, majority vote would pick 1975, but if our consensus module has learned that the Knowledge Guru is usually right on factual date questions, it might assign a higher score to 1976 despite it being a minority. This can correct the majority when the majority is likely wrong.

We emphasize that our consensus optimization is lightweight – it does not require modifying the large language models themselves and can be viewed as a post-processor. Yet, as results will show, it contributes noticeable gains in final accuracy.

To illustrate how the learned consensus improves factual reasoning, consider a GSM8K case where two Solver agents incorrectly agreed on 125, while the Checker agent argued for 120 with detailed arithmetic justification. The consensus module correctly assigned higher weight to the Checker’s reasoning, yielding the correct answer (120). However, we also observed occasional failure cases – for instance, when multiple Knowledge Guru agents dominated the vote, leading to over-reliance on factual recall and overlooking logical consistency. These cases suggest that while role-weighted aggregation improves reliability, it may also introduce role-specific bias if not balanced.

For future work, we plan to explore more interpretable consensus scoring, such as visualizing agent confidence via heatmaps or tracing justification overlaps among reasoning paths. Such analysis could make the decision process of the consensus module more transparent to human evaluators.

Finally, one could consider a more complex approach where the debate doesn’t end with a vote, but rather the agents collectively write a single answer (like a panel writing a joint report). We experimented with prompting one agent to “summarize the debate and give the final answer,” which is akin to having a designated judge agent. This worked well for simple cases but sometimes introduced bias (if the judge was itself an LLM, it might favor certain phrasing). Therefore, our primary method uses the learned voting scheme for clarity and reliability. An interesting future direction is to train an LLM explicitly as a debate judge on transcripts, which could combine well with our weighted voting.

With the methodology explained, we next turn to the experimental setup and results, demonstrating the impact of each component of A-HMAD on various benchmarks.

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Datasets

We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the proposed A-HMAD framework on multiple benchmarks that test arithmetic reasoning, mathematical problem solving, factual question answering, and strategic game reasoning. In total, we cover six benchmarks:

-
Arithmetic Expressions: a set of synthetic arithmetic problems (evaluating expressions of integers with basic operations), which test basic calculation and order-of-operations reasoning.

-
Grade School Math (GSM8K): a benchmark of 8,000 diverse grade-school level math word problems requiring multi-step reasoning (Cobbe et al. 2021). We use the official test split and report accuracy of the final answer.

-
Massive Multi-Task Language Understanding (MMLU): a collection of 57 subjects testing world knowledge and reasoning, aggregated into a single accuracy score (Hendrycks et al. 2020). We evaluate on the dev set of MMLU (which is standard for model comparisons) using 5-shot prompting for the single-agent baseline, as is common (Hendrycks et al. 2020).

-
Chess Problem Solving: two tasks related to chess gameplay:

-
Move Validity: Given a chess position and a proposed move in algebraic notation, determine if the move is legal/valid. This tests rule-based reasoning and attention to detail (as models often hallucinate illegal moves in chess).

-
Move Optimality: Given a chess position, choose the optimal move. We use a subset of tactical puzzles where one move leads to a win; optimality is measured by comparing the model’s move to the engine (Stockfish) best move (Du et al. 2023). We report a normalized score (100 means always optimal, 0 means always worst among options).


-
-
Factual Biographies: a dataset of short biographies of famous computer scientists, where models must fill in factual details (affiliations, awards, dates) correctly (Du et al. 2023). This tests factual accuracy in a generation setting. Following (Du et al. 2023), we evaluate the factual correctness of each generated biography by checking key facts against ground truth (accuracy averaged across facts).


### 4.2 Evaluation metrics

We use standard classification metrics:

-
**Accuracy**: the percentage of correct predictions. This is appropriate for 20NG (balanced classes) and EduQA (slightly imbalanced, but we will report macro-average as well). -
**Macro F1-Score**: especially for EduQA where classes might not be exactly equal, macro-F1 gives equal weight to each class’s performance, which is important if some classes are harder. -
We also consider

**ROC AUC**for binary tasks like MRPC/RTE (though in multi-class it’s less common). -
For robustness analysis, we will report metrics like accuracy under perturbation and stability (percentage of predictions unchanged by specific perturbations).


We first describe our experimental setup, baseline implementations, and metrics. Then we present results for: (1) Main performance comparison on all tasks (A-HMAD vs baselines), (2) Ablation studies on heterogeneity and consensus weighting, (3) Effect of number of agents and debate rounds, (4) Case study examples illustrating how A-HMAD debates proceed.

### 4.3 Experimental setup

### Models (agents)

Unless otherwise specified, our agents are based on the LLaMA model (Hurst et al. 2024), which is a strong open-source LLM with instruction-following tuning (comparable to GPT-3.5 in capability). We choose this to replicate conditions similar to Du et al. (2023) (who used GPT-3.5 for most experiments) while having more control over model internals if needed. For certain experiments, we also use OpenAI’s GPT-4 API as an “expert agent” or for comparison. Each agent runs on one 80GB A100 GPU, and multi-agent inference is parallelized when possible.

### Baselines

We compare A-HMAD against several baselines::

-
**Single Agent (Direct)**: A single LLaMA answering the question without chain-of-thought (i.e. greedy generation of the answer). -
**Single Agent (Zero-Shot CoT)**(Kojima et al. 2022): A single agent with a “Let’s think step by step” style prompt (Kojima et al. 2022) to induce reasoning. The answer is then extracted from the chain-of-thought. -
**Single Agent (Few-Shot CoT)**(Wei et al. 2022): The agent given 5 exemplars of CoT reasoning (for tasks where such data is available, e.g. we use samples from GSM8K training set) as prefix. This tests prompt-tuning via demonstrations. -
**Single Agent (Reflection)**(Kawamura et al. 2003; Madaan et al. 2023): The agent is allowed to output an initial answer and reasoning, then is prompted with “Are there any mistakes? Please reflect and try again.” We allow one reflection iteration (which was sufficient to see improvements). -
**Single Agent (Self-Consistency Ensemble)**(Irving et al. 2018): We sample 5 independent chain-of-thought solutions from the single agent (by varying random seed) and take the majority answer. -
**Multi-Agent (Majority Vote)**: The original debate method (Kojima et al. 2022) with 3 homogeneous agents (LLaMA-2 70B-chat) debating for 2 rounds and final answer by majority vote. This is the primary baseline representing prior state-of-art in multi-agent prompting. -
**Liang et al. (2023) Divergent Debate**(Kadavath et al. 2022): A variant of debate where two agents with different prompts debate one round. We use their method of “encouraging divergent thinking” in a pair of agents and then combine answers by voting. -
**No Debate, 3-Model Majority**: As an ablation, we have 3 independent agents answer without debating and take majority vote. This isolates the effect of debate vs just having an ensemble.

### Metrics

Our primary metric is accuracy: percentage of questions answered correctly. For open-generation like biographies, we break down accuracy per factual attribute. For chess optimality, we convert Stockfish’s evaluation of the chosen move into a score (if the model’s move is the top engine move, score 100; if it’s a blunder losing the game, score 0; intermediate moves get intermediate scores proportional to win probability). We also track the consensus rate in multi-agent runs – how often all agents ended up with the same final answer – as an indicator of debate convergence. Additionally, we record the number of debate rounds used (which can vary in A-HMAD due to dynamic stopping).

Each result is averaged over a set of test queries (100 for arithmetic, the full 1319 GSM8K test, MMLU dev 5k questions, 50 chess puzzles each, and 50 biographies). We report mean and standard deviation (±) where appropriate, especially for smaller sets or where sampling is involved.

### 4.4 Main results

Table 1 presents the accuracy of all methods on the six benchmarks. We highlight A-HMAD and the original Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) baseline for comparison.

Key observations:

-
A-HMAD achieves the highest accuracy on all tasks among competing methods. For instance, on GSM8K, it reaches 90.2%, an absolute +6.2% over the original MAD and +13.2% over single-agent self-consistency. This is a new state-of-the-art for reasoning on this dataset with a 70B-class model (comparable to GPT-4’s 92% which is a 180B+ model).

-
On MMLU, A-HMAD hits 76.5%, which is 5.4 points above MAD’s 71.1%. This indicates our method’s benefits extend to multi-domain knowledge QA. Notably, our single-agent few-shot baseline was 63.9%, so debate provided a +12.6 point boost, and our enhancements added further +5.4.

-
For arithmetic, all methods do quite well, but A-HMAD’s 87.5% is the highest. The arithmetic tasks are simple enough that even reflection or self-consistency were above 75%. The remaining errors often involve edge cases or slight format issues.

-
Chess Move Validity sees a near-ceiling performance for debate methods: MAD had 95%, and A-HMAD 98%. Single LLMs were around 72–79%. The debate (with an agent role focusing on rule-checking) almost eliminates illegal moves. The last few percent errors are typically very nuanced rules (like castling rights) that even debate might miss without an external chess engine.

-
Chess Move Optimality is improved from 85 \(\rightarrow \) 91 by A-HMAD. The margin here is smaller but still substantial. This task is challenging because it requires strategic depth – the debate helps by allowing agents to cross-verify lines of play. A-HMAD’s slight edge may come from an agent we include that specifically enumerates opponent responses (a “Devil’s Advocate” chess agent).

-
Biographies factual accuracy: out of an average of 5 key facts per biography, single LLM had 60% correct, MAD raised it to 74%, and A-HMAD to 80.6%. This means each biography on average had one fewer incorrect fact with our method compared to a single model. Human-written Wikipedia-level biographies would be 95% by our metric, so there is still a gap, but our method substantially closes the gap relative to single LLM.


Overall, A-HMAD yields 4–7% absolute improvements over the prior state-of-the-art multi-agent debate across tasks, confirming the effectiveness of our proposed innovations. All improvements are statistically significant (\(p<0.01\) by a paired bootstrap test on the sample of questions). The largest gain was on GSM8K (+6.2%), which we attribute to the strong complementary skills of our Solver and Checker agents in complex math reasoning. The smallest gain was on Chess Validity (which was near-solved by baseline already, leaving little room).

To ensure fairness, we also measured the compute cost of each method. A-HMAD with dynamic routing used on average 2.3 rounds and 3 agents per question, which is slightly higher than the fixed 2-round, 3-agent MAD baseline. This led to about 1.3\(\times \) the inference time of MAD. However, due to skipping irrelevant agents for many questions (e.g., not using the Knowledge agent on math problems), A-HMAD’s cost did not blow up despite added complexity. We argue this moderate overhead is justified by the significant accuracy gains. In scenarios where compute is constrained, one could limit A-HMAD to 2 rounds max or fewer agents; we examine the effect of such modifications next.

### 4.5 Ablation study

We perform controlled experiments to isolate the contribution of each component: heterogeneity of agents and the learned consensus. We also analyze the impact of the number of agents and debate rounds. All ablations are on a subset of tasks (Arithmetic, GSM8K, MMLU) for computational efficiency, using 100 questions from each.

title: X-MAS: Towards Building Multi-Agent Systems with Heterogeneous LLMs
description: Proposes heterogeneous multi-agent LLM systems powered by diverse LLMs for specialization, extending beyond single-LLM constraint to elevate system intelligence.
content:
# X-MAS: Towards Building

Multi-Agent Systems with Heterogeneous LLMs

###### Abstract

LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) extend the capabilities of single LLMs by enabling cooperation among multiple specialized agents. However, most existing MAS frameworks rely on a single LLM to drive all agents, constraining the system’s intelligence to the limit of that model. This paper explores the paradigm of heterogeneous LLM-driven MAS (X-MAS), where agents are powered by diverse LLMs, elevating the system’s potential to the collective intelligence of diverse LLMs. We introduce X-MAS-Bench, a comprehensive testbed designed to evaluate the performance of various LLMs across different domains and MAS-related functions. As an extensive empirical study, we assess 27 LLMs across 5 domains (encompassing 21 test sets) and 5 functions, conducting over 1.7 million evaluations to identify optimal model selections for each domain-function combination. Building on these findings, we demonstrate that transitioning from homogeneous to heterogeneous LLM-driven MAS can significantly enhance system performance without requiring structural redesign. Specifically, in a chatbot-only MAS scenario, the heterogeneous configuration yields up to 8.4% performance improvement on the MATH dataset. In a mixed chatbot-reasoner scenario, the heterogeneous MAS could achieve a remarkable 47% performance boost on the AIME dataset. Our results underscore the transformative potential of heterogeneous LLMs in MAS, highlighting a promising avenue for advancing scalable, collaborative AI systems.

## 1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) such as GPT [1], Gemini [2], Qwen [3], have been applied across various domains. However, despite their remarkable capabilities, LLMs often struggle with multifaceted, complex, and real-world problems due to inherent limitations such as hallucinations [4, 5].

In response to these limitations, LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have emerged as a promising solution [6, 7, 8]. MAS involves the collaboration of multiple agents, each specialized in specific functions, to address problems more effectively than a single model could. his paradigm has been successfully applied across various scenarios, including software development [7, 9], mathematics [10, 11], and scientific discovery [12, 13]. For instance, ChatDev [7], MetaGPT [9], and EvoMAC [14] utilize multiple coding agents (e.g., coders and testers) to improve software programming, while AI co-scientist [8] employs a MAS to enhance biomedical and scientific research.

Despite notable progress, most existing MAS frameworks rely on a single LLM to drive all agents [9, 7, 11, 6, 14, 15, 16]. This manner inherently limits the system’s intelligence to that of the underlying model. For example, if a single LLM produces fundamental errors in certain facts, these mistakes are unlikely to be corrected through the collaboration of agents powered by the same model. Inspired by the advantages of diversity in collective intelligence [17, 18, 19], this paper explores MAS with heterogeneous LLMs (X-MAS), pushing the system’s capabilities beyond its previous limit to harness the collective potential of LLMs trained on diverse corpora or by different teams [20, 21, 22].

To provide a comprehensive evaluation of LLMs in MAS, we introduce X-MAS-Bench, a testbed designed to assess the performance of various LLMs across different MAS-related functions and domains. Specifically, we consider 5 representative functions of agents in MAS, including question-answering [15, 9], revise [14, 23], aggregation [24, 25], planning [26, 10], and evaluation [16, 7]; as well as 5 common domains, including mathematics, coding, science, medicine, and finance—spanning 21 test sets. Each function is assessed under controlled experimental conditions. For example, when assessing aggregation, each query is input into several pre-defined LLMs, whose outputs are concatenated to be aggregated by the examined LLM. The aggregated responses of various LLMs are then evaluated and compared. Finally, we assess 27 LLMs across these 5 functions and 5 domains, conducting over 1.7 million evaluations to identify the optimal model selections for each domain-function combination. Our findings include that (1) no single LLM excels across all scenarios, (2) a single LLM could have significant performance variation across functions and domains, (3) different LLMs may show large performance disparities within the same function and domain, (4) smaller LLMs can sometimes outperform larger ones, highlighting the potential advantages of employing heterogeneous LLMs in MAS. These results provide valuable insights for researchers and practitioners in selecting the most appropriate LLMs for their specific MAS applications.

Building on these observations, we explore the effects of transitioning from homogeneous to heterogeneous LLM-driven MAS (X-MAS-Design). As a proof of concept, given the implementation of a MAS method, we simply assign agents with appropriate LLMs (taking seconds) by referring observations in X-MAS-Bench. To validate our idea, we examine three existing MAS frameworks—LLM-Debate [15], AgentVerse [16], and DyLAN [11]—as well as a prototype MAS designed by us, which incorporates all five functions in one system. Our analysis covers five domains with no sample overlap compared to X-MAS-Bench. In a chatbot-only scenario, we observe consistent improvements in performance for heterogeneous MAS over homogeneous configurations, achieving up to a 8.4% performance gain on the MATH [27] benchmark. Interestingly, while reasoner-only MAS often underperforms relative to chatbot-only systems, combining chatbot and reasoner in a heterogeneous MAS leads to significant performance improvements. Specifically, in the competition-level AIME-2024 benchmark, AgentVerse [16] is improved from 20% to 50%, and DyLAN [11] improved from 40% to 63%. Our further experiments reveal that increasing the number of candidate LLMs for heterogeneous MAS results in a monotonic performance improvement, reinforcing the value of LLM diversity in MAS. Based on our work, future research could explore more nuanced strategies for selecting and integrating LLMs in heterogeneous MAS; investigate the scalability and adaptability of heterogeneous MAS across different industries and other complex tasks.

Our contributions are as follows:

-
1.
X-MAS-Bench: We assess 27 LLMs across 5 MAS-related functions and 5 domains, conducting over 1.7 million evaluations to identify diverse optimal model selections for each domain-function combination. These observations could benefit researchers and practitioners in building MAS.

-
2.
X-MAS-Design: Based on findings in X-MAS-Bench, we propose to transition existing MAS methods from homogeneous to heterogeneous LLM-driven MAS. We conduct extensive experiments, showing that heterogeneous MAS consistently outperforms homogeneous MAS.

-
3.
Open Source: We release all data, code, and evaluation results to facilitate future MAS research.


## 2 Related Work

LLM-based MAS. LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) leverage multiple LLM-based agents to collaborate for better task solving than single LLM [16, 9, 28, 6]. ChatDev [7], MetaGPT [9], and EvoMAC [14] use multiple coding agents (e.g., coders and testers) for software programming; while MACM [10] applies math agents for mathematics. Focusing on general tasks, debate-based methods [15, 25] enable multiple experts in debating for better solutions; AgentVerse [16] and DyLAN [11] dynamically adjust the agent team for task solving; while MAS-GPT [6] trains an LLM for generating MAS. However, all of these methods rely on a single LLM to drive all agents, which inherently limits the system’s intelligence to that of the underlying LLM. This paper proposes to push the limit by harnessing the collective intelligence of heterogeneous LLMs from different sources.

Heterogeneous LLMs. In a general context of LLMs, there are several works related to using heterogeneous LLMs [29, 30]. LLM-Blender [31] trains a model for ensembling outputs from multiple LLMs. MoA [32] and ReConcile [33] enable multiple LLMs for discussion, however, involving all candidate LLMs without considering their appropriateness. MASRouter [34] manually selects several candidate LLMs for MAS and is optimized for their specific framework. In contrast, our paper systematically assess the capabilities of LLMs across several MAS-related functions and domains, aiming to universally benefit the design of heterogeneous MAS for various MAS methods.

Benchmarking LLMs. Many works benchmark the capabilities of LLMs in various domains (such as math [27], coding [35], science [36], medicine [37], and finance [38]) and functions (such as planning [39] and evaluation [40]). However, our paper for the first time benchmarks LLMs for MAS, which assesses the capabilities of LLMs across 25 function-domain perspectives related to MAS.

## 3 X-MAS-Bench: Evaluating LLMs for MAS

X-MAS-Bench is a testbed designed to assess the performance of various LLMs across different MAS-related functions and domains. Specifically, we consider 5 representative functions of agents in MAS—question-answering [15, 9], revise [14, 23], aggregation [24, 25], planning [26, 10], and evaluation [16, 7]. Orthogonally, we investigate behaviors in 5 domains, including mathematics, coding, science, medicine, and finance—spanning 21 test sets. Each function is assessed under controlled experimental conditions. In this section, we demonstrate the details of experimental conditions in Section 3.1 and experimental results in Section 3.2.

### 3.1 Benchmarking MAS-Related Functions

To systematically assess LLM capabilities in a multi-agent context, we decompose MAS behaviors into five representative and commonly-used agent functions: question-answering, revise, aggregation, planning, and evaluation. For each function, we define a standardized prompt protocol. In all cases, we carefully control experimental conditions such that the only varying factor is the LLM under evaluation. Below we detail the designed assessment of each function.

Question-answering. The question-answering (QA) function measures a LLM’s ability to comprehend a question and produce a correct answer in free-text form. This function is fundamental to all MAS methods such as LLM-Debate [15], where each agent first independently answers the query, and to MetaGPT [9], in which an agent supplies initial draft responses in first stage of the processing. In QA assessment, LLM receives a sampled query from any test dataset (e.g., MATH [27]) as input and returns an answer in free-text format. The outputs are compared with ground-truth answers, where the resulted accuracy will be the indicator to assess the QA ability.

Revise. The function of revise assesses an agent’s capacity to revise an initial answer, which is potentially flawed, to produce a corrected answer. This function commonly exists in workflows requiring iterative refinement, such as the update agent in EvoMAC [14] and the refiner in Self-Refine [23]. In assessment of revise, given a prompt formatted with a sampled query and a corresponding answer generated by a pre-defined LLM, the examined LLM is asked to provide a final complete answer by reasoning and revising over the provided query and answer. In this case, all examined LLMs are provided with the same prompt (i.e., sourced from the same query and same pre-defined LLM), therefore ensuring fair comparisons among examined LLMs. Similarly, the revised outputs are compared with ground-truth answers and the resulting accuracy denotes the revise capability.

Aggregation. Aggregation refers to the capability of combining multiple candidate answers into a coherent, correct, and even improved final answer. It is a key mechanism in MAS that leverages multiple answering paths, such as convergent agents in MacNet [24], and extractive mode of the judge in MAD [25]. To assess aggregation, for each query, we collect candidate responses from a fixed set of pre-defined LLMs (set to 3 in this case). The examined LLM is provided with the query and these candidate responses in a fixed concatenated format, and is asked to synthesize the final answer. Importantly, all candidate responses and their order remain identical across all models, ensuring consistency in the prompts and allowing for fair comparisons. The aggregated answers are then scored against the ground-truth answers using accuracy as the metric.

Planning. Planning involves decomposing a task into sub-tasks and assigning appropriate roles to agents along a workflow to solve the problem collaboratively. This function is critical in systems like MACM [10] and MapCoder [26], where a thinker or a planning agent defines the entire agentic workflow. In planning assessment, the task of the examined LLM is to provide a suitable plan to the sampled query by giving the role descriptions of the agents required to answer the query together with the workflow, whose output should follow a pre-defined format for subsequent string extraction. Subsequently, the ordered role descriptions and the number of roles are extracted. Next, the corresponding number (i.e., role number) of candidate LLMs are activated for action according to the role description and workflow arrangement. Input prompts and candidate LLMs are kept fixed across all examined LLMs. The overall system performance—evaluated by final task accuracy—serves as the proxy for planning capability.

Evaluation. Evaluation measures an agent’s ability to critically assess the quality or correctness of other agents’ outputs. This function is used in MAS to filter faulty reasoning, select better solutions, determine early stopping, or guide further actions—commonly seen in frameworks like AgentVerse [16] and ChatDev [7]. In our assessment, each examined LLM is presented with a query and an answer generated by a pre-defined LLM. The examined LLM is instructed to determine whether the provided answer correctly address the query. The candidate answer and evaluation instruction remain constant across LLMs to ensure fair comparison. Unlike the evaluation in previous functions, the judgment of the examined LLM is compared against ground-truth correctness.

### 3.2 Experiments in Evaluating LLMs across Functions and Domains

Following the above definitions of functions, this section assesses the capabilities of various LLMs in different functions and domains, aiming at demonstrating the landscape of LLMs for MAS. The reported results are expected to demonstrate the potential of leveraging heterogeneous LLMs for MAS and facilitate future researchers in choosing appropriate LLMs for their MAS.

Experimental setups. We examine 27 LLMs, covering 20 chatbots (i.e., instructed LLMs) and 7 reasoners (i.e., reasoning LLMs). Among the 20 chatbots, we consider general chatbots trained by different companies such as Llama [21], Qwen [20], Mistral [41, 42], and domain-specific chatbots including mathematics [22], coding [43], science [44, 45], medicine [46, 47], and finance [46, 47]. The reasoners include LLMs from DeepSeek [48], Qwen [49], and others [50]. We set each model’s maximum token limit to its own capacity, 8192 tokens maxed, with a temperature of 0.5 by default. Specially, all LLMs instantiated within the planning workflow are executed with their temperature fixed at 0 to guarantee as the planning involves format-following. Our datasets cover domains including mathematics [27, 51, 52, 53, 54, 55], coding [56, 57, 58], science [36, 59, 60, 61], medicine [62, 63, 64], and finance [65, 66, 67], where each dataset is randomly sampled up to 500 examples without replacement; see more details in Section C.
