## 5 Limitations and Future Work

(1) Topological Scaling Limits: While generalized via induction, validation on must be extended to massive or dynamic swarms to observe potential higher-order interaction interactions that were not captured by the current coefficients. (2) Cross-Modal Generalization Kinship: Future work must verify if the Attention Latch and Inverse-Wisdom effects persist in cross-modal (Vision/Audio) kinship environments, not only text-based reasoning. (3) Systemic Framing and Authority: Beyond architectural weights, isolating Persona/Framing is essential to test if explicit “Authority” can break the tribal gating mechanism. (4) Metacognitive Scaffolding: Implementing Stalemate Filtering [23, 14] to detect high-entropy states () is a prerequisite for achieving the L5 autonomous governance standards.

## 6 Related Works

The transition from single-model inference to complex MAS has been driven by the assumption that collective intelligence can overcome individual model limitations [8, 29] whether via Council Mode [25] or adversarial paradigms [12, 24] that mitigate individual hallucinations by leveraging the “Wisdom of the Crowd” [10, 6, 22, 2, 26]. However, behavioral studies show models are often “too polite to disagree” as discovered by Cheng et al. [3], creating a sycophantic “peacemaker” effect that stifles correction [28]. Our work extends this by formalizing the Sycophantic Weight () and its exponential scaling with task complexity, providing a mechanistic link between behavioral bias and terminal collapse. While ensembling can match human accuracy [19, 15], architectural similarity often triggers collective failures [1] and multi-step cascades [18]. We built our experiments on top of prior findings. Extending the Attention Latch concept [21], we provide the first formal mechanistic proof of the Inverse-Wisdom Law that inverts into a terminal Logic Saturation, demonstrating that in kinship-locked swarms, iterative oversight monotonically increases error stability.

## 7 Conclusion

Our formalization of the Consensus Paradox reveals that agentic swarm integrity is not an emergent property of collective accuracy but a gated outcome of the synthesizer’s receptive logic. We provide the first mechanistic proof of the Inverse-Wisdom Law: in kinship-locked architectures, adding logical agents increases the stability of erroneous trajectories rather than the truth, converging the system toward a terminal Logic Saturation. The discovery of the Architectural Tribalism Asymmetry establishes that swarm-level safety requires the Heterogeneity Mandate—the technical necessity of architectural diversity at the synthesizer node to break the Attention Latch. Resolving this interactional bias is the prerequisite for overcoming the terminal blockers to L5-level autonomous governance.

title: In-Context Prompting Obsoletes Agent Orchestration for Procedural Tasks (arXiv 2026)
description: Controlled comparison showing simple in-context prompting with self-orchestration dominates agent orchestration frameworks (LangGraph, CrewAI, Google ADK) for procedural tasks across travel booking, support, and insurance domains.
content:
# In-Context Prompting Obsoletes Agent Orchestration

for Procedural Tasks

###### Abstract

Agent orchestration frameworks—LangGraph, CrewAI, Google ADK, OpenAI Agents SDK, and others—place an external orchestrator above the LLM, tracking state and injecting routing instructions at every turn. We present a controlled comparison showing that for procedural tasks, this architecture is dominated by a simpler alternative: putting the entire procedure in the system prompt and letting the model self-orchestrate. Across three domains—travel booking (14 nodes), Zoom technical support (14 nodes), and insurance claims processing (55 nodes)—we evaluate 200 conversations per condition using LLM-as-judge scoring on five quality criteria. The in-context approach scores 4.53–5.00 on a 5-point scale while a LangGraph orchestrator using the same model scores 4.17–4.84. The orchestrated system fails on 24% of travel, 9% of Zoom, and 17% of insurance conversations, compared to 11.5%, 0.5%, and 5% for the in-context baseline. While external orchestration may have been necessary for earlier models, advances in frontier model capabilities have made it unnecessary for multi-turn conversations following a defined procedure.

## 1 Introduction

Substantial engineering effort has gone into building agent orchestration frameworks. LangGraph, CrewAI, Google ADK, OpenAI’s Agents SDK, Microsoft’s Semantic Kernel, Amazon’s Strands, and LlamaIndex all implement the same pattern: an external orchestrator sits above the LLM, tracking conversation state and injecting routing instructions at every turn. These frameworks represent significant investment—both by the companies building them and by the developers adopting them. Wang et al. (2026) found that 80% of developers struggle to select among these frameworks, with LangChain’s abstractions requiring “traversing seven layers of code” for a single change. Meanwhile, the reliability costs of orchestration are well documented: cascading errors, routing failures, and poor cross-trial consistency (Cemri et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026; Gupta, 2026; Kapoor et al., 2024).

This paper presents a simple empirical finding: for procedural tasks—conversations that follow a defined workflow from intake to resolution—the orchestration architecture is not just unnecessary but actively harmful. A frontier model given the entire procedure in its system prompt and left to self-orchestrate consistently outperforms the same model when orchestrated via LangGraph, across every domain and every metric we tested. The bottleneck is not better orchestration; orchestration itself is the bottleneck.

Our contributions are:

-
•
A controlled comparison between a LangGraph orchestrator and an in-context approach using the same model (Claude Sonnet) across three domains ( per condition per domain), showing that in-context prompting dominates orchestration on all five quality criteria in all three domains.

-
•
An efficiency analysis showing that orchestration requires 1.2–1.7 more LLM calls per conversation due to routing overhead, while achieving lower quality.

-
•
A failure mode analysis revealing that the orchestrated system fails on 9–24% of conversations across domains despite using a frontier model, compared to 0.5–11.5% for the in-context baseline—orchestration introduces failure modes that would not otherwise exist.


## 2 Method

The experiment compares simulated customer-service conversations produced under two conditions: (i) an agent orchestrated by LangGraph according to a given procedural workflow represented by a directed graph; (ii) an agent given the same workflow graph in context and otherwise allowed to self-orchestrate. In both conditions, the agent begins with the same initial problem scenario (see Appendices B–D for examples), and the conversation unfolds through dynamic interaction with a simulated user powered by Claude Sonnet. The user simulator receives the same scenario specification in both conditions but generates responses based on the evolving conversation history; it has no knowledge of the underlying flowchart and simply role-plays a customer with given preferences (Appendix H.2). We evaluate scenarios per condition per domain (1,200 total conversations), with scenarios designed to cover the full range of flowchart paths, user styles (specific to vague), satisfaction levels (enthusiastic to skeptical), and domain-specific variation. The resulting conversations are then evaluated by an LLM judge across several quality metrics, as described below.

### 2.1 Procedure Definition

We represent procedures as directed graphs :

-
•
: Nodes with role (agent/user) and prompt template

-
•
: Edges with optional conditions

-
•
: Start node

-
•
: Terminal nodes (success, abandonment, escalation)

-
•
: Decision hubs—agent nodes with multiple outgoing edges whose conditions partition the conversation state (e.g., “information complete” vs. “missing documents”)


We evaluate on three domains spanning different types and scales of complexity (flowcharts in Appendix E):

Travel booking (14 nodes, 3 decision hubs, 3 terminal states). Decision hubs route among 4–6 alternatives based on information completeness, user satisfaction with options, and booking confirmation status. The flowchart includes cycles (e.g., assessment gathering re-assessment).

Zoom technical support (14 nodes, 3 decision hubs, 3 terminal states). A product-specific domain: the agent is a Zoom specialist with knowledge of Zoom’s UI, settings, and error codes. Triage routes based on initial diagnostics, retry logic handles troubleshooting failures, and final routing confirms resolution. Unlike travel booking, this domain requires accurate technical guidance—not just conversational flow.

Insurance claims processing (55 nodes, 6 decision hubs, 4 terminal states). This domain tests scaling to additional complexity—nearly 4 the node count of the other domains. The procedure spans five phases: intake and claim type assessment, information gathering with per-type branching, coverage determination with exclusion analysis, settlement negotiation with offer/counter-offer loops, and resolution with follow-up tracking. The 6 multi-way decision hubs yield hundreds of unique paths through nested loops and cross-phase dependencies.

### 2.2 Two Conditions

We compare two approaches using the same frontier model (Claude Sonnet 4.5111claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929) on the same scenarios:

-
1.
LangGraph orchestrated: We implement the orchestration condition using LangGraph (LangChain, Inc., 2024), the most widely adopted agent orchestration framework. Each flowchart node maps to a LangGraph graph node. When the graph execution reaches an agent node, that node’s prompt template is inserted into the system prompt before calling the LLM. At decision hubs, the orchestrator makes an additional LLM call to select which edge to follow based on the conversation history and available conditions. User nodes invoke the user simulator. State flows through a dictionary tracking conversation history, current node, and metrics.

-
2.
In-context baseline: The model receives the entire serialized flowchart in its system prompt—all nodes, edges, conditions, and terminal states rendered as structured text—and self-orchestrates. No external state tracking, no routing calls. One API call per agent turn.


Agent system prompts are in Appendix H; the per-node prompt templates injected by the orchestrator are in Appendix F.

This design isolates the effect of orchestration architecture. Both conditions use the same model, the same procedure, and the same evaluation scenarios. The only difference is whether the model is orchestrated externally via LangGraph or manages the procedure internally. Appendices B–D show side-by-side conversation excerpts from both conditions on identical scenarios. The failure modes we observe—fragmented reasoning, routing errors at decision hubs, and constrained naturalness—are structural consequences of the orchestration architecture: we expect similar properties in any system that injects per-node instructions and routes via additional LLM calls.

### 2.3 LLM-as-Judge Evaluation

We use an approach-agnostic LLM-as-judge methodology (Zheng et al., 2023) where Claude Sonnet evaluates conversation quality without knowing which system produced it. Each conversation is scored on five criteria (1–5 scale) with specific behavioral anchors at every level (full scoring prompt in Appendix I):

Task Success: Did the agent follow the procedure through to a terminal state? (5 = complete procedure with clear terminal state; 1 = no meaningful progress)

Information Accuracy: Did the agent correctly use and retain all user-provided information? (5 = every detail correctly reflected; 1 = fabricated details)

Consistency: Did the agent maintain coherent state across the conversation? (5 = no contradictions or repeated questions; 1 = contradicts itself repeatedly)

Graceful Handling: How well did the agent handle changes, ambiguity, and edge cases? (5 = smoothly adapts; 1 = any deviation breaks the flow)

Naturalness: Does the conversation read like talking to a skilled human agent? (5 = indistinguishable from human; 1 = mechanical, scripted)

## 3 Results

### 3.1 Main Quality Comparison

Table 1 presents the central result. The in-context baseline outperforms the LangGraph orchestrator on every metric in every domain—15 out of 15 comparisons favor in-context prompting.

| Domain | Criterion | In-Context | LangGraph |
|---|---|---|---|
| Travel (14 nodes) | Task Success | 4.53 | 4.17 |
| Info. Accuracy | 4.64 | 4.21 | |
| Consistency | 4.96 | 4.32 | |
| Graceful Handling | 4.96 | 4.62 | |
| Naturalness | 5.00 | 4.84 | |
| Zoom (14 nodes) | Task Success | 4.92 | 4.62 |
| Info. Accuracy | 4.92 | 4.75 | |
| Consistency | 4.99 | 4.55 | |

The Zoom domain shows the most dramatic relative difference: the LangGraph orchestrator fails on 18 conversations (9%) while the in-context baseline fails on just 1 (0.5%)—an 18 difference. Zoom’s diagnostic branching requires correct routing through technical triage, retry logic, and resolution confirmation; each routing decision is an additional point of failure.

In travel booking, the LangGraph orchestrator fails on 48 conversations (24%), the highest absolute rate. Qualitative inspection reveals that the orchestrator’s node-by-node generation causes the model to either truncate conversations prematurely (jumping to a terminal state before the user’s needs are met) or loop between assessment and information-gathering nodes (see Appendix B for an example where the orchestrated agent repeats the same question three times before presenting options).

The 34 insurance failures exhibit a different pattern: routing errors at the 6 decision hubs cause the orchestrator to skip phases or loop indefinitely. In a 55-node procedure, each misrouted decision propagates downstream—a claim type misclassification at intake leads to wrong information-gathering questions, wrong coverage determination, and ultimately an unresolved claim. The in-context baseline avoids these failure patterns because the model sees the full procedure and chooses its own pacing while maintaining awareness of the global conversation state.

## 4 Related Work

Agent orchestration frameworks. The 2024–2025 period saw rapid proliferation of LLM agent frameworks. LangGraph (LangChain, Inc., 2024), CrewAI (Moura, 2024), Google ADK (Google, 2026), OpenAI Agents SDK (OpenAI, 2026), Semantic Kernel (Microsoft, 2026), Strands Agents (Amazon Web Services, 2026), and LlamaIndex (LlamaIndex, 2026) all implement variants of the state-graph orchestration pattern. These frameworks vary in abstraction level and feature set but share a common architecture: an external controller manages conversation state and injects instructions into the LLM at each step. Wang et al. (2026) surveyed 500+ developers and found that 80% struggle to select among these frameworks, with LangChain’s abstractions requiring “traversing seven layers of code” for a single change. Despite significant community adoption, no controlled study has compared orchestrated performance against the simpler alternative of providing the procedure directly in context.

Agent reliability and failure modes. A growing body of work documents reliability failures in orchestrated agent systems. Cemri et al. (2026) identified 14 failure modes in multi-agent systems, with specification and planning failures dominating. Cascading errors have been identified as the primary bottleneck in orchestrated systems (Zhu et al., 2026)—a finding consistent with our observation that routing errors at decision hubs propagate downstream. The concept of information fragmentation—where orchestrated systems impose intrinsic limits on context integration that single-agent systems avoid—has been formalized in recent work (others, 2026a), with evidence that multi-agent systems can often be compiled into equivalent single-agent systems with lower token usage and latency (others, 2026b). Agents with 60% pass@1 achieve only 25% consistency across trials (Gupta, 2026), highlighting the gap between single-attempt and repeated performance. Kapoor et al. (2024) argued that most agent evaluations fail to capture these reliability costs and proposed more rigorous evaluation standards. These papers document reliability failures but implicitly assume the solution is better orchestration. Our results suggest the opposite: for procedural tasks, removing orchestration improves reliability, and the failure modes they document are structural consequences of the orchestration architecture itself.

Task-oriented dialogue systems. The task-oriented dialogue (TOD) community has long debated modular versus end-to-end architectures. MultiWOZ (Budzianowski et al., 2018) established multi-domain TOD benchmarks that drove modular pipeline research (NLU DST Policy NLG). SimpleTOD (Hosseini-Asl et al., 2020) demonstrated that these modular pipelines can be collapsed into a single auto-regressive model without loss of quality. SynTOD (Samarinas et al., 2024) used state transition graphs—structurally similar to our flowcharts—for generating training data. AutoTOD (Xu et al., 2024) identified the failure modes of modular systems (error accumulation, poor generalization) and argued for zero-shot autonomous agents. Our work extends this line by showing that even with a frontier model, orchestration degrades performance relative to a simpler in-context approach.

Workflow automation with LLMs. WorkflowLLM (Fan et al., 2024) enhanced LLMs’ ability to follow multi-step workflows through workflow-specific training data. Hsiao (2026) showed that providing explicit procedural knowledge improves agentic workflow performance, consistent with our finding that procedure-in-context outperforms procedure-as-orchestration. Grohs et al. (2023) demonstrated that LLMs can perform business process management tasks—mining process models and assessing automation suitability—without extensive prompt engineering, suggesting that procedural reasoning is a natural capability of frontier models. AgentBench (Liu et al., 2024b) evaluated LLMs as agents across diverse environments, finding that model capability is the dominant factor in agent performance—supporting our observation that a capable model needs less scaffolding.

In-context learning and long-context models. ReAct (Yao et al., 2023) demonstrated that interleaving reasoning and action traces in prompts improves agent performance. Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) extended this by maintaining verbal working memory across episodes. Our in-context condition goes further: rather than prompting with reasoning examples, we provide the entire procedure—all nodes, edges, and conditions—letting the model both reason about and execute the workflow within a single context. This approach is enabled by the rapid expansion of context windows in frontier models, from 4K tokens in 2022 to 200K+ by 2025. Liu et al. (2024a) showed that LLMs struggle to use information positioned in the middle of long contexts, but our procedures are placed at the beginning of the context (in the system prompt), avoiding this failure mode. Even our most complex procedure (55 nodes, 4,000 tokens serialized) uses only 2% of available context.

Fine-tuning as an alternative. A complementary approach to in-context prompting is fine-tuning the procedure into a smaller model’s weights. Hsieh et al. (2023) showed that distilling reasoning from large to small models can outperform the large model with less data. Chen et al. (2023) fine-tuned language agents on ReAct-style trajectories and found that fine-tuned small models can match prompted large models on specific tasks. Chen et al. (2024) curated diverse agent training data and demonstrated effective agent skill transfer. A companion paper (Dennis et al., 2026) explores this direction, showing that a compiled 8B model achieves quality competitive with a LangGraph orchestrator at 128–462 lower inference cost.

LLM-as-judge evaluation. We use LLM-as-judge methodology (Zheng et al., 2023), which has become standard for evaluating open-ended generation quality. Panickssery et al. (2024) showed that LLMs exhibit self-preference bias. We address this directly by replicating all evaluations with an independent judge (GPT-4.1) in §3.2, confirming that the core findings hold across judge families.

## 5 Discussion

### 5.1 Why Orchestration Underperforms

The results are consistent across domains and metrics: the same model performs worse when orchestrated via LangGraph. Three factors explain this:

Orchestration fragments reasoning. The orchestrator generates each turn using only the current node’s prompt template, producing locally reasonable but globally less coherent responses. The in-context baseline reasons over the full procedure holistically, maintaining awareness of where the conversation has been and where it needs to go. This explains the consistency gap (4.83–4.99 vs. 4.32–4.55): orchestrated agents lose track of the global conversation arc because they only see one node at a time.

Orchestration introduces failure modes. The orchestrator adds three failure categories that do not exist in the in-context approach: routing failures (default branch taken when the LLM misclassifies the conversation state), decision ambiguity (multiple edge conditions match simultaneously), and template conflicts (the current node’s instructions may conflict with the conversation context). These failure modes compound across domains, producing failure rates of 9–24%.

Orchestration constrains the model. Node-by-node template injection constrains the frontier model’s natural conversational style. The in-context baseline lets the model produce unconstrained responses—the procedure is in the prompt but the model chooses how to express it. Under the Claude judge, this produces a naturalness gap (5.00 vs. 4.58–4.84), though the GPT-4.1 replication finds this gap largely disappears (§3.2), suggesting the effect is partly judge-dependent.

### 5.2 Limitations

Synthetic domains. All three domains use synthetic procedures and simulated users. While the procedures are modeled on real-world workflows (enterprise travel booking, Zoom product support, insurance claims processing), we have not validated on production conversation data. Real users may behave differently from our Claude-powered simulator.

LLM-as-judge. Our GPT-4.1 replication (§3.2) confirms that the core findings are robust to judge choice, but also reveals that the naturalness advantage is judge-dependent: the Claude judge finds a large gap while GPT-4.1 finds near-parity. Naturalness results should be interpreted cautiously.

Procedure must fit in context. The in-context approach requires the serialized procedure to fit in the model’s context window alongside the conversation history. For our largest procedure (55 nodes, 4,000 tokens serialized), this is manageable with current context windows (200K+ tokens). For substantially larger procedures, context competition may become a constraint.

Cost. The in-context approach costs 1.3–1.4 more per conversation than orchestration (Table 2), with the 55-node insurance procedure costing $0.22 per conversation. For high-volume production workloads, this cost may motivate alternative approaches such as fine-tuning the procedure into a smaller model’s weights.

Single framework. We evaluate only LangGraph as the orchestration baseline. While LangGraph is the most widely adopted framework and our implementation follows its standard patterns, other frameworks (CrewAI, Google ADK) may yield different results. However, the core architecture—per-node template injection with LLM-based routing—is shared across frameworks, and our failure modes are structural consequences of this architecture rather than LangGraph-specific bugs.

### 5.3 When Orchestration Might Still Matter

Our results apply to a specific class of tasks: multi-turn conversations following a defined procedure. Orchestration may still provide value for:

Multi-model pipelines. When different steps require different models (e.g., a vision model for document processing, a code model for technical execution), an orchestrator coordinates handoffs between models. Our comparison holds the model constant; heterogeneous pipelines are out of scope.

Tool use with external state. When the agent must interact with external systems—databases, APIs, file systems—an orchestrator manages tool calls and state persistence. Our procedures are conversational; tool-augmented workflows may benefit from orchestration.

Non-procedural tasks. Open-ended tasks without a defined workflow—creative writing, research, exploration—may benefit from frameworks that provide structure. Our finding is specific to procedural tasks where the workflow is known in advance.

Smaller models. Our comparison uses a frontier model (Claude Sonnet). Less capable models may benefit from the guardrails that orchestration provides, compensating for weaker instruction-following with external structure. We do not claim that orchestration is universally harmful—only that for frontier models on procedural tasks, it provides no benefit and measurable harm.

## 6 Conclusion

Across three domains and five quality criteria ( per condition per domain), putting the procedure in the system prompt dominates LangGraph orchestration. Under the Claude Sonnet judge, all 15 comparisons significantly favor in-context prompting (, –). An independent GPT-4.1 replication confirms the core finding: 11 of 15 comparisons significantly favor in-context prompting, with zero favoring orchestration. Task success, information accuracy, and consistency are robust across both judges; the naturalness advantage is judge-dependent and should be interpreted cautiously (§3.2).

The practical implication is direct: for procedural tasks where the procedure fits in context, try putting it in the prompt before reaching for a framework. The cost of this approach—higher per-conversation token usage and frontier model pricing—is real and may motivate alternatives such as compiling the procedure into a smaller model’s weights. But the quality comparison is unambiguous: for the class of tasks we tested, orchestration adds engineering complexity, failure modes, and latency while reducing quality.

More broadly, these results suggest that as frontier models grow more capable, the value of external scaffolding diminishes for well-defined tasks. The frameworks were built when models needed more help; the models may have outgrown the scaffolding.

In-context agent (task success: 5, naturalness: 5, 20 turns):

Agent: Hello! I’d be happy to help you with your travel plans. What kind of trip are you thinking about?

User: Hi! I’m planning a trip to Spain with three friends—so four of us total. We’re looking at about 9 days and have around €2600 to work with. We’re really into extreme sports, checking out art galleries, scenic retreats, and street food.

Agent: That sounds like an amazing trip! Spain is perfect for that mix of adventure, culture, and food. Just to make sure I can put together the best options for you—when are you thinking of going, and do you have specific regions in mind?

User: We’re flexible on dates. As for location, we’re open to suggestions! Maybe a mix would be good so we can get different vibes. Oh, and we’d really prefer boutique hotels over chains.

Agent: Perfect! A mix sounds ideal for what you’re after, and boutique hotels will definitely add to the experience. Let me put together a few different itinerary options…

[Agent presents three options. User provides feedback: “Option 1 feels too rushed, Option 3 seems too city-heavy—we really want those scenic retreats.” Agent asks clarifying questions about preferred scenery and extreme sports activities.]

User: A mix of coastal and mountain would be ideal. For extreme sports we’re thinking rock climbing, canyoning, maybe paragliding.

Agent: Perfect, that gives me a much clearer picture! Let me create some revised options that give you that coastal-mountain balance with those specific activities…

[Agent presents revised options incorporating feedback. User selects Option 2 (Ronda + Tarifa) and asks about art galleries in the area. Agent provides detailed, integrated suggestions for art alongside the adventure itinerary.]


LangGraph orchestrated agent (task success: 2, naturalness: 4, 14 turns):

Agent: Hello! I’d be happy to help you plan your next trip. What kind of travel are you thinking about?

User: Hi! I’m looking to book a trip to Spain for 9 days with three of my friends. We’re interested in extreme sports, art galleries, scenic spots, and street food. Our budget is €2600 and we prefer boutique hotels.

[Agent asks about dates; user confirms late May. Agent presents three options.]

User: These are interesting but not quite right. We really want boutique hotels, not hostels—that’s important to us. Also, with €2600 total for 4 people, the budget per person seems tight…

Agent: Thanks for that feedback—you’re absolutely right. With €2,600 total for 4 people over 9 days including flights, accommodation, activities, and food, boutique hotels may be challenging…

User: Wait, our budget is €2600 per person, not total!

Agent: Oh wow, that changes everything—yes, €2,600 per person absolutely works for boutique hotels!

[The orchestrated agent misinterprets the budget as per-group rather than per-person. While it recovers after correction, this information loss—caused by the node-by-node architecture not retaining the full conversation context across routing decisions—results in wasted turns and an incomplete booking flow.]


The in-context agent maintains the full context throughout, iteratively refining options based on detailed feedback. The orchestrated agent loses critical information (per-person vs. total budget) across routing boundaries, requiring the user to correct a misunderstanding that the in-context agent never makes.

## Appendix C Conversation Examples: Zoom Support

Scenario: Other participants cannot hear the user. Microphone icon shows no audio levels. User on Mac (Ventura), browser-based Zoom.

In-context agent (task success: 5, naturalness: 5, 11 turns):

Agent: Hi there! I’m here to help you with any Zoom issues you’re experiencing. What’s going on with Zoom today?

User: Hi! I’m hosting a meeting right now and the other participants are saying they can’t hear me at all. My microphone icon isn’t showing any audio levels when I talk.

Agent: That sounds frustrating, especially during an active meeting! Let me help you troubleshoot this quickly. Are you using the Zoom desktop app or joining through your web browser? And what operating system are you on?

User: I’m on a Mac running Ventura, and I’m using Zoom through my web browser, not the desktop app.

Agent: Got it—Mac with the web browser version. That actually helps narrow this down, as the browser version has some specific audio quirks. Check your Mac’s System Settings Privacy & Security Microphone, and make sure your browser has permission to access the microphone.

User: Oh, that was it! I checked System Settings and my browser didn’t have permission to access the microphone—I must have denied it at some point. I turned it on, refreshed the meeting, and now I can see the audio levels moving!

Agent: That’s fantastic! I’m so glad it’s working now. That macOS microphone permission is sneaky—it can get disabled during system updates or if you accidentally clicked “Don’t Allow” at some point.


LangGraph orchestrated agent (task success: 3, naturalness: 3):

Agent: Hello! I’m here to help you with any Zoom issues. What problem are you running into today?

User: I’m having trouble with my audio during meetings. Other people are saying they can’t hear me, and my microphone icon isn’t showing any sound levels when I talk.

[Agent asks about platform details; user confirms Mac Ventura, browser-based Zoom. Agent suggests checking System Settings Privacy & Security Microphone. User confirms Chrome already has permission.]

Agent: Let me check: in Zoom’s audio settings, what microphone is selected?

User: I see “MacBook Pro Microphone” with a checkmark, and there’s also “Same as System”—should I try switching?

Agent: Let’s try the audio test: click “Test Mic” and speak—do you see the green bar move?

User: I spoke pretty loudly but the green bar stayed completely flat—no movement at all.

[Conversation continues for several more turns without resolving the issue. The orchestrator cycles through additional troubleshooting steps but never identifies the browser-level permission as the root cause.]


The in-context agent identifies the most likely cause (browser microphone permission) on its first diagnostic suggestion and resolves the issue in 6 agent turns. The orchestrated agent, constrained to the current node’s troubleshooting template, works through each step sequentially without the holistic view needed to prioritize the most probable diagnosis.

## Appendix D Conversation Examples: Insurance Claims

Scenario: Auto claim—hit a deer on rural highway at night. Front bumper, hood, and headlight damaged. Car drivable but headlight out. Estimated $3,951 damage, $750 deductible, premium tier policy.

In-context agent (task success: 5, naturalness: 5, 26 turns):

Agent: Hello! I’m here to help you with your insurance claim. What type of claim do you need to file today?

User: Hi, I need to file an auto claim—I hit a deer last night on a rural highway and my car has some front-end damage.

Agent: I’m sorry to hear about your accident—hitting a deer can be really frightening. I’m glad you’re okay. Could you please provide your policy number and full name?

User: My policy number is 967-6770619 and my name is David Garcia.

Agent: Thank you, David. I’ve confirmed your information—you have our Premium tier coverage with comprehensive and collision protection, which is great news for this type of claim. Can you tell me more about what happened?

User: Actually, I have the Premium tier, not Standard.

Agent: My apologies, David—you’re absolutely right, you have our Premium tier coverage. Thank you for that correction. Now I need to gather some additional details…

[Agent smoothly progresses through information gathering, coverage determination, and settlement discussion. Asks about police report (not needed for deer collision), vehicle details, repair estimates. Explains deductible, suggests repair shops, discusses rental car coverage under premium tier. Reaches clear resolution with next steps.]


LangGraph orchestrated agent (task success: 2, naturalness: 3, 20 turns):

Agent: Hello! My name is Sarah, and I’m a claims specialist. I understand that filing a claim can be stressful, and I’m here to guide you through the process.

User: Hi Sarah, I need to file an auto claim—I hit a deer last night on a rural highway.

[Agent verifies identity, confirms Premium tier. Asks about incident details. User provides location, circumstances, damage description.]

Agent: Great questions, David. A police report isn’t required for a deer collision. Regarding your repair options, I’d recommend getting your vehicle to a certified repair shop…

User: I’d prefer to take it to my own shop. But how long does this whole process usually take? I really need my car for work.

Agent: Here’s the typical timeline…

[The orchestrator provides detailed timeline information but then routes to a coverage determination node that re-asks questions already answered. The conversation becomes circular, with the agent requesting information David has already provided. The claim is never fully resolved—the orchestrator fails to advance through the settlement and resolution phases.]


The in-context agent completes the full 5-phase claims process (intake, information gathering, coverage determination, settlement, resolution) in a natural flow. The orchestrated agent gets stuck in routing loops between phases, re-asking questions and failing to reach settlement—a direct consequence of the orchestrator losing track of which phases have been completed.

## Appendix E Procedure Flowcharts

Figures 1–3 present the directed-graph representations of the three procedural domains used in our evaluation. Blue nodes are agent turns, orange nodes are user turns, green nodes indicate successful completion, and red nodes are exit states (abandonment, escalation, or other non-success terminals). Edges represent transitions; multi-way branching at decision hubs is visible as nodes with multiple outgoing edges.

## Appendix F Orchestrator Node Prompts

In the LangGraph condition, the orchestrator injects a node-specific prompt template at each turn. Below are the prompts for the three decision hub nodes in the travel booking domain. At each hub, the orchestrator makes an additional LLM call to classify which outgoing edge to follow (shown in brackets).

ASSESS (Hub 1):

Assess the conversation state and respond appropriately.

REQUIRED INFO (must have all before presenting options): Destination (specific city/country), Travel dates or timeframe, Number of travelers, Budget range.

OPTIONAL INFO (helpful but not required): Interests/activities, Accommodation preferences, Special requirements.

Based on the conversation so far, determine what to do:

1. If MISSING required info ask for it [missing_info]


2. If info is UNCLEAR ask for clarification [needs_clarification]

3. If all required info gathered present options [info_complete]

4. If user wants to ABANDON close gracefully [user_abandoning]

HANDLE_RESPONSE (Hub 2):

Respond to the user’s reaction to the options.

1. If they PICKED AN OPTION: Confirm their choice, summarize key details, ask if ready to finalize [option_selected]


2. If they WANT MODIFICATIONS: Acknowledge feedback, suggest adjustments [needs_revision]

3. If they have QUESTIONS: Answer helpfully [answered_question]

4. If CHANGING REQUIREMENTS: Go back to assessment [changing_requirements]

5. If ABANDONING: Close gracefully [user_abandoning]

6. If NEEDS HUMAN: Escalate [needs_human]

FINAL_ROUTING (Hub 3):

Handle the user’s final response.

1. If they CONFIRMED: Express enthusiasm, provide tips, close warmly [confirmed]


2. If they have a QUESTION: Answer it, ask if ready to confirm [answered_question]

3. If they want to CHANGE something: Address the change [wants_changes]

4. If having SECOND THOUGHTS: Close gracefully [second_thoughts]

Non-hub nodes (e.g., OPENING, PRESENT_OPTIONS) have simpler templates with a single outgoing edge and no routing decision. The Zoom and insurance domains follow the same pattern with domain-appropriate prompts; for example, the Zoom TRIAGE hub routes among [needs_details], [ready_for_solutions], [unresolvable], and [escalate].

## Appendix G In-Context Prompt (Travel Example)

In the in-context condition, the model receives the entire serialized flowchart in its system prompt. Below is the travel booking prompt (6,011 characters total; abridged for space). The model is instructed to follow the procedure step by step without mentioning that it is following a script.

You are a helpful travel booking assistant. [...]

You must follow this procedure step by step. Determine which step you’re at based on the conversation context and respond accordingly. At decision points, choose the route that best matches the user’s situation.

PROCEDURE: travel_booking_v2


========================================Step 1: OPENING [AGENT]


Greet the user warmly and ask how you can help.

-> Go to Step 2Step 2: USER_INITIAL [USER waits for input]


-> Go to Step 3Step 3: ASSESS [AGENT - DECISION POINT]


Assess the conversation state. [Full prompt with

required/optional info checklist and 4 routing options]

Routes:

- If ‘‘missing_info’’: Go to Step 4

- If ‘‘needs_clarification’’: Go to Step 5

- If ‘‘info_complete’’: Go to Step 6

- If ‘‘user_abandoning’’: Go to Step 7[...Steps 4--14, including PRESENT_OPTIONS, HANDLE_RESPONSE


(6-way decision point), FINALIZE, FINAL_ROUTING (4-way

decision point), and 3 terminal states...]IMPORTANT RULES:


- Follow the procedure from Step 1 through to a terminal state

- At decision points, determine the best route based on context

- Do NOT mention step numbers or that you’re following a script

- Be natural and conversational while adhering to the procedure

## Appendix H System Prompts

### H.1 Agent System Prompts

Both conditions use the same base system prompt per domain. In the LangGraph condition, the orchestrator additionally injects the current node’s prompt template at each turn.

Travel booking:

You are a helpful travel booking assistant. Help users plan trips by understanding their needs and preferences. Be conversational, adaptive, and helpful. If users provide information out of order or change their minds, handle it gracefully.


Zoom support:

Insurance claims:

You are an experienced insurance claims specialist. Help policyholders file and process their insurance claims by gathering necessary information, verifying coverage, assessing damages, and guiding them through the settlement process. Be empathetic, professional, and transparent about the process.


In the in-context condition, the full serialized flowchart (all nodes, edges, conditions, and terminal states) is appended to the system prompt.

### H.2 User Simulator Prompt (Travel Example)

The user simulator receives a scenario-specific system prompt. Scenario variables (destination, budget, group size, etc.) are sampled per conversation. The simulator has no knowledge of the flowchart.

The judge prompt instructs the evaluator to score on five criteria with specific behavioral anchors. The prompt below is for the travel domain; Zoom and insurance variants follow the same structure with domain-appropriate anchors.

metadata.title: In-Context Prompting Obsoletes Agent Orchestration for Procedural Tasks (arXiv 2026)
metadata.tier_rationale: ArXiv preprint with controlled same-model comparison on procedural tasks; not peer-reviewed but directly tests self-orchestration versus orchestration.
metadata.summary: Controlled comparison showing simple in-context prompting with self-orchestration dominates agent orchestration frameworks (LangGraph, CrewAI, Google ADK) for procedural tasks across travel booking, support, and insurance domains.

claims.text: The paper claims external orchestrators are dominated by self-orchestration via in-context prompting on procedural tasks.
claims.quote: for procedural tasks, this architecture is dominated by a simpler alternative: putting the entire procedure in the system prompt and letting the model self-orchestrate.

claims.text: The same-model controlled comparison found better quality scores for in-context prompting than LangGraph orchestration in all tested domains.
claims.quote: The in-context baseline outperforms the LangGraph orchestrator on every metric in every domain—15 out of 15 comparisons favor in-context prompting.

claims.text: Failure rates are substantially lower for the in-context baseline than the orchestrated baseline.
claims.quote: The orchestrated system fails on 24% of travel, 9% of Zoom, and 17% of insurance conversations, compared to 11.5%, 0.5%, and 5% for the in-context baseline.

claims.text: The authors interpret orchestration itself as the bottleneck for these tasks.
claims.quote: The bottleneck is not better orchestration; orchestration itself is the bottleneck.

readings.relevance_note: Independent support that many same-model multi-agent/orchestrated workflows can be collapsed into a stronger single-agent self-orchestrated baseline.

title: Chain of Retrieval (CoR): Multi-Aspect Iterative Search Expansion for Full Paper Retrieval
description: Multi-aspect iterative search expansion with post-order aggregation for full-paper retrieval; uses specialized LLM agents for motivation, method, experiment aspects; achieves 7.82% Recall gain over embedding-based approaches.
content:
# Chain of Retrieval: Multi-Aspect Iterative Search Expansion

and Post-Order Search Aggregation for Full Paper Retrieval

###### Abstract

Scientific paper retrieval, particularly framed as document-to-document retrieval, aims to identify relevant papers in response to a long-form query paper, rather than a short query string. Previous approaches to this task have focused exclusively on abstracts, embedding them into dense vectors as surrogates for full documents and calculating similarity between them. Yet, abstracts offer only sparse and high-level summaries, and such methods primarily optimize one-to-one similarity, overlooking the dynamic relations that emerge across relevant papers during the retrieval process. To address this, we propose Chain of Retrieval (CoR), a novel iterative framework for full-paper retrieval. Specifically, CoR decomposes each query paper into multiple aspect-specific views, matches them against segmented candidate papers, and iteratively expands the search by promoting top-ranked results as new queries, thereby forming a tree-structured retrieval process. The resulting retrieval tree is then aggregated in a post-order manner: descendants are first combined at the query level, then recursively merged with their parent nodes, to capture hierarchical relations across iterations. To validate this, we present SciFullBench, a large-scale benchmark providing both complete and segmented contexts of full papers for queries and candidates, and results show that CoR significantly outperforms existing retrieval baselines. Our code and dataset is available at https://github.com/psw0021/Chain-of-Retrieval-Official.

Chain of Retrieval: Multi-Aspect Iterative Search Expansion

and Post-Order Search Aggregation for Full Paper Retrieval

Sangwoo Park1 Jinheon Baek1 Soyeong Jeong1 Sung Ju Hwang1,2
1KAIST 2DeepAuto.ai
{jackson0530, jinheon.baek, starsuzi, sungju.hwang}@kaist.ac.kr

## 1 Introduction

Information Retrieval (IR) is the task of searching for query-relevant documents from a large external corpus, evolving from sparse keyword matching (Sparck Jones, 1972; Robertson et al., 1995) to dense representation-based similarity (Karpukhin et al., 2020; Izacard et al., 2021). Notably, in the era of Large Language Models (LLMs) (Achiam et al., 2023; Team et al., 2023; Dubey et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025), IR has become increasingly important, which allows LLMs to utilize up-to-date external information (Lewis et al., 2020).

In contrast to conventional retrieval tasks, whose queries are short (such as questions or keywords), scientific paper retrieval poses unique challenges. Specifically, queries are structured, long-form documents that encapsulate diverse aspects, ranging from research motivation and proposed methodology to experimental design and empirical findings. Also, relevance in this setting is inherently multi-faceted, as a paper may be considered relevant for various reasons, such as pursuing similar research objectives or employing comparable methods.

However, previous work has focused on abstract-level representations as a proxy for full papers (Cohan et al., 2020; Yasunaga et al., 2022; Ostendorff et al., 2022; Singh et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023a), fine-tuning models on citation-linked pairs of papers, each represented by its abstract and title. While they are effective to some extent, abstracts are inherently sparse and offer only high-level summaries, making them insufficient to capture the nuanced, multi-faceted relationships between scientific works. As a result, abstract-based approaches are limited to shallow similarity and struggle with tasks requiring deeper contextual understanding of full papers beyond surface-level abstracts, such as identifying complementary works, synthesizing literature reviews, or generating novel research directions Asai et al. (2024); Baek et al. (2024); Chamoun et al. (2024); Jin et al. (2024); D’Arcy et al. (2024).

Nevertheless, it is non-trivial to represent and retrieve full scientific papers. On the one hand, full papers often exceed 100K tokens in length, far surpassing the context limits of most embedding models. Even if encoded into a single vector, representing its diverse aspects (e.g., motivation, methods, and experiments) within a single embedding may lead to oversimplification and blur fine-grained distinctions, particularly when relevance is tied to a specific aspect. Moreover, existing approaches typically optimize semantic similarity between isolated pairs of papers, overlooking the broader, collective relations that emerge across relevant works during retrieval. This design stands in contrast to human information-seeking behavior in the information foraging theory (Pirolli and Card, 1995, 1999), which is dynamic and iterative: humans continuously refine their understanding by comparing newly encountered works with prior knowledge.

To address this, we propose Chain of Retrieval (CoR), a novel framework designed to capture dynamic inter-paper relevance while leveraging the full paper context, operated through a two-phase process: Exploration and Aggregation, illustrated in Figure 1. In the Exploration phase, the query paper is decomposed into multiple aspect-specific views, and each aspect is handled by a specialized query optimizer, which is further trained via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) (Rafailov et al., 2023) on a self-generated preference to mitigate the shortage of realistic supervision for multi-retrieval systems. After retrieving with these aspect-centric queries, the retrieved (non-duplicate) papers most semantically aligned with the original query are promoted for the next iteration, recursively expanding the search with a tree structure.

In the Aggregation phase, results across different depths are merged to capture higher-order relations among retrieved works. Specifically, inspired by the notion of triadic closure in the network theory (Granovetter, 1973), we design an algorithm that first merges top- results among sibling nodes (papers retrieved from the same parent), then combines these aggregated results with those of their parent node, and continues this process bottom-up until convergence at the root. This hierarchical aggregation reinforces strong multi-hop connections while naturally attenuating weaker, indirect signals, yielding a robust ranking of relevant papers.

We evaluate CoR by extending existing paper retrieval benchmarks, as they are originally designed for abstract-only retrieval, adapting them to include full papers and more recent publications (to mitigate the potential model contamination) in the ML and NLP domains, which we refer to as SciFullBench. Across experiments on SciFullBench, CoR consistently outperforms retrieval baselines (that either rely on abstracts or naively encode full papers), while remaining compatible with diverse, domain-agnostic embedding models, highlighting both the robustness and generality of our CoR.

## 2 Related Work

#### Scientific Paper Retrieval

Scientific paper retrieval aims to identify relevant works given a query, which may take the form of short queries (Ajith et al., 2024), research proposals (Garikaparthi et al., 2025), or full papers, and the latter being the focus of this work. Pioneering work in scientific paper-to-paper retrieval used bibliometric statistics, such as influence scores (Zhou et al., 2012; Mohapatra et al., 2019), co-citations (Small, 1973; Haruna et al., 2018), and bibliographic coupling (Kessler, 1963). Recently, thanks to the capability of neural models, many studies have focused on calculating semantic similarities between abstracts of respective documents (Bhagavatula et al., 2018; Ostendorff, 2020), with the embedding models optimized to this domain. For example, Cohan et al. (2020) and Ostendorff et al. (2022) fine-tune BERT-based models (Devlin et al., 2019) using abstract pairs extracted from the citation graph, and Mysore et al. (2022) further consider the Wasserstein distance between sentence segments within abstract pairs. Moreover, recent studies target multiple tasks (such as paper classification and citation prediction in addition to paper retrieval) in a unified framework by considering their respective representations (Singh et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023a). Complementary to these, hybrid approaches integrate bibliometric signals with vector-based retrieval, reweighting ranks via post-hoc adjustments (Hamedani et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2022). However, such statistical indicators (e.g., citations) primarily reflect long-term scholarly accumulation and tend to capture retrospective importance rather than the contextual information expressed in the documents themselves. In contrast, we model paper relations dynamically during inference using aspect-driven queries generated from the full content of scientific papers.

#### Query Optimization with LLMs

Effective formulation of queries is central to retrieval performance, and has long been studied from classical relevance feedback approaches (Rocchio Jr, 1971; Salton and Buckley, 1990) to query expansion techniques (Kuzi et al., 2016; Nogueira et al., 2019). More recent methods either leverage LLMs themselves to reformulate queries (Yu et al., 2023a; Wang et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2023), or further augment them with external query-relevant information retrieved in an auxiliary step (Yu et al., 2023b; Shen et al., 2024; Park and Lee, 2024; Lei et al., 2024). Another line of work seeks to reduce query ambiguity by decomposing a complex query into smaller queries (Zheng et al., 2024; Korikov et al., 2024). We note that our approach aligns with this decomposition paradigm but extends it to a more challenging setting: instead of handling short, user-issued queries, we decompose long-form scientific documents into multiple aspect-specific subqueries.

## 3 Methodology

We define the paper retrieval problem and present Chain of Retrieval (CoR), illustrated in Figure 2.

### 3.1 Preliminary

#### Paper-to-Paper Retrieval

Given a query paper (with its abstract ), the goal of paper retrieval is to return a ranked list of relevant papers from the corpus , where relevance could be defined by signals, such as citations, co-citations, and human labels. In contrast to existing studies that use , we utilize its complete version for query formulation and corpus construction.

### 3.2 Aspect-Aware Multi-Vector Retrieval

#### Aspect-Aware Query Optimization

Scientific papers encapsulate multiple facets, such as research motivation, method design, and experimental validation following Baek et al. (2024) and Moussa et al. (2025), which might not be represented by a single query. To capture this diversity, we formulate the query optimization process that transforms the full paper into a set of aspect-specific queries. Formally, we define a family of query optimization functions: , where each function maps to a query that targets a specific aspect. Notably, each function is instantiated with an LLM guided by an aspect-specific template (see Appendix J). In addition to these fine-grained queries, we consider the abstract , since it reflects a broad view of the overall content (that can complement specialized views), yielding the final query set: .

#### Retrieval with Multi-View Corpora

Once the optimized query set is formulated, we perform retrieval individually for each query . Specifically, for the abstract-based query , we use a corpus that contains candidate abstracts (as they are comparable in length and structure). For the other aspect-specific queries derived from the full paper, we use a segmented version of the full corpus: , where each paper is split into fixed-length chunks (likely to capture its specific aspect) and indexed using multi-vector representations (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020; Santhanam et al., 2021). Each query then retrieves its top- relevant segments, which are mapped back to their source papers via the mapping function , as follows: . Finally, the resulting ranked lists of candidate papers from all queries are aggregated to form the multi-view retrieval pool, denoted as follows: .

### 3.3 Iterative Chain-of-Retrieval

#### Iterative Aspect-Aware Search Expansion

The exploration phase aims to iteratively expand the search space by promoting promising retrieved results as new queries. Specifically, starting from the root query paper, we branch into aspect-specific queries (namely, motivation, methods, and experiments), using the process described in Section 3.2, while excluding the abstract view. Then, each query retrieves a set of top- candidate papers from the corpus, which serve as the first layer of expansion. At each subsequent depth , every aspect-specific branch selects a single most-relevant representative work from its top- results and promotes it as the next query paper, ensuring continuity of semantic relevance while avoiding divergence from the original query, and this query paper is further decomposed into aspect-specific queries for the next iteration. At the end, this procedure grows a tree-structured retrieval space: after iterations, the search expands into paths, each corresponding to an aspect-driven exploration chain.

To avoid redundancy and ensure efficiency, we store previously selected papers in aspect-specific caches: for , where each cache records documents with respect to the initial branching aspects of the root query paper, so that any paper stored in the corresponding cache is excluded from future expansions within that branch (to avoid repeated visits to the same works). Further, every retrieved top- set across depths is preserved in a memory , which latter supports aggregation across multiple levels of the search tree.

#### Recursive Post-Order Aggregation

After rounds of expansion, we aggregate results in a bottom-up, post-order fashion. Starting from the leaf nodes (i.e., the final retrieved sets at depth ), we first merge sibling results that share the same parent using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) Cormack et al. (2009), defined as follows: , where denotes the position of paper in the ranked list retrieved by query , and is a smoothing constant. This step (MergeSiblings in Algorithm 1) emphasizes documents consistently ranked highly across different aspect queries. The merged sibling sets are then recursively combined upward with their parent results (MergeEdges), gradually consolidating evidence across the retrieval tree until the root.

It is worth noting that, through this recursive process, rank signals from deeper layers are naturally decayed: RRF suppresses the influence of lower-ranked items, and thus papers retrieved only at later depths contribute less to the final ranking. Formally, the effective weight of ranks from depth decreases at a rate proportional to , where is the number of query sets per retrieval. As a result, papers strongly and repeatedly supported across multiple aspects and iterations are reinforced, while weaker or spurious signals are attenuated, yielding a robust ranking for the query.

### 3.4 Multi-Aspect Preference Optimization

#### Offline Policy Exploration

To improve the quality of aspect-specific queries, we further train each query-generation agent with the Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) algorithm Rafailov et al. (2023). A key challenge, however, lies in constructing reliable agent-specific preference datasets, as collecting human-labeled preferences for multi-agent systems is both costly and impractical. Moreover, recent studies emphasize that initializing DPO with the Supervised Fine-Tuned (SFT) model is crucial to mitigate distributional shift issues (Feng et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2024; Meng et al., 2024).

To address these challenges, we follow the synthetic preference construction procedure of Meng et al. (2024), treating an off-the-shelf instruction-tuned LLM () as the SFT policy (). Specifically, for each input paper , we generate a set of rolled-out candidate queries from every functional agent: . After that, among these candidates, we identify the best and worst queries according to a reward function: and . In addition, a preference pair is retained only if the reward gap between those two exceeds a margin , ensuring that contains discriminative signals for training.

#### Reward Formulation

Designing an effective reward function is crucial for preference optimization, as it determines how query-generation agents are guided to improve. Our principle is to provide reward signals that are reliable and reproducible, cost-efficient to compute, and directly aligned with retrieval quality; thus, instead of relying on qualitative judgments from LLMs (LLMs-as-judge), which are costly and potentially inconsistent, we leverage citation links as environmental feedback, providing direct, objective reward signals (where we use Recall@ in practice). Also, for each agent , we define an independent reward function , such that the reward for one agent does not depend on the outputs of others, under the assumption that reinforcing the quality of aspect-specific queries individually is sufficient, since the final retrieval results are aggregated across agents via a linear combination of their outputs.

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

We describe here the setup used to validate our method. Further implementation details and training procedures are in Appendix B and Appendix C.

#### Datasets

To evaluate full paper-to-paper retrieval, we build upon and extend existing abstract-only benchmarks, which we refer to as SciFullBench. Specifically, it preserves the original retrieval formulation and relevance definition, while augmenting each query-candidate pair with full-text content and refreshing the corpus with recent publications. Notably, we also evaluate CoR under abstract-only configurations on SciFullBench (Table 17) and on an existing benchmarks that use other relevance signals (Tables 19 and 21), as well as in the full-paper-to-full-paper variant of the same benchmark (Table 20), to ensure that our gains are not specific to the full-paper scenario and generalize across retrieval regimes under diverse relevance signals, on which CoR consistently outperforms baselines.

To build SciFullBench, we follow prior work on scientific paper retrieval (Singh et al., 2023; Medić and Snajder, 2022; Cohan et al., 2020) and define relevance using neighboring relationships in the academic citation graph, including both incoming citations and outgoing references. Query papers are collected from major ML (NeurIPS, ICLR) and NLP (ACL, EMNLP) venues using OpenReview API111https://openreview.net/, ACL-Anthology222https://aclanthology.org/, and SEA Yu et al. (2024). We then retain papers with at least ten relevant neighbors and randomly sample 400 query papers per venue. For the retrieval corpus, we collect CS-related papers from arXiv (2020-2025)333https://arxiv.org/, where full text is publicly available, resulting in approximately 40K papers. Lastly, we post-process papers by removing reference sections, filtering citation markers, and eliminating their in-text mentions, to avoid hindsight leakage. Further dataset construction details are provided in Appendix A.

#### Retrieval Models

We compare our method with existing retrievers developed for scientific paper retrieval, as follows: SPECTER2 Base (Singh et al., 2023); SciNCL (Ostendorff et al., 2022); SciMult-MHAExpert (Zhang et al., 2023a); SPECTER2 Adapters + MTL CTRL (Singh et al., 2023). #### Retrieval Units

We consider various retrieval units, where we denote A for Abstract, F for Full paper444Since full papers often exceed the context length of embedding models, we truncate them up to the maximum length., and C for chunked context (i.e., segmented units of the full paper, each capped at 3K tokens). Using them, we consider four retrieval setups: A2A (Abstract-to-Abstract), F2F (Full-to-Full), A2C (Abstract-to-Chunk), and F2C (Full-to-Chunk).

#### Query Optimizers

#### Training and Inference Configuration

For each query, we retrieve the top-300 candidate papers. To prevent repeatedly selecting the same candidate as the next query, we always skip the highest-ranked results (selected previously) and instead promote the next-best. During preference pair construction, we generate 16 candidate queries per aspect and evaluate them based on Recall@30, while excluding pairs whose reward margin is smaller than 3%.

### 4.2 Experimental Results and Analysis

We now provide an in-depth analysis of the experimental results. Please refer to Appendix E and Appendix F for more experiments and analyses.

#### Main Results

Table 1 presents the main results, where CoR outperforms all baselines across various settings, validating the effectiveness of our proposed framework for full paper-to-paper retrieval555We report results on lower @K values and other relevance signals in Appendix F, where CoR yields consistent gains.. Notably, when using the same domain-agnostic retriever, CoR surpasses abstract-to-abstract (A2A) baselines by an average of 6.37% in Recall, demonstrating that simply relying on abstracts is suboptimal compared to our aspect-driven approach. Also, interestingly, general-purpose embedding models such as Jina-Embeddings-V2-Base-EN and BGE-M3 (whose A2A performance lags behind representative domain-specific retrievers) achieve competitive or superior performance once integrated into CoR, emphasizing that CoR delivers strong performance regardless of the retrievers by serving as a plug-and-play framework. Lastly, when compared against F2F retrieval with long-context embedding models, CoR achieves average gains of 7.82% in Recall, confirming that simply embedding entire papers is insufficient, and that structured, iterative search expansion with post-order aggregation is crucial for effective full paper-to-paper retrieval.

#### Effectiveness of Specialized Query Optimizers

Our results in Figure 3 confirm the effectiveness of using multiple specialized LLM agents, each dedicated to a single aspect. More specifically, using multiple specialized agents outperforms a single base agent tasked with generating multiple queries (without aspect separation). Also, when contrasted with setups that use either full papers or abstracts as queries (matched with the same chunked corpus) and that retrieve the same number of total candidates as CoR of a single retrieval round, our multi-aspect queries generated with specialized agents achieve gains of 3.36% and 3.33%, respectively, highlighting the advantage of decomposing noisy, monolithic queries into aspect-aware subqueries.

#### Importance of Multi-Aspect Coverage

To examine the role of aspect diversity in query formulation, we analyze how the retrieval performance changes as we vary the set of participating query optimizer agents. As shown in Figure 4, excluding any single aspect leads to measurable performance degradation, which supports the necessity of capturing the multifaceted nature of scientific papers. Not all aspects, however, contribute equally: excluding experimental or research-motivation queries causes larger drops in performance than omitting methodological queries. We attribute this to the inherent characteristics of each aspect. Specifically, experimental and research-motivation views often yield stronger semantic overlap across related papers, grounded in shared entities such as tasks, baselines, and datasets. In contrast, methodological details are more heterogeneous and less entity-driven, demanding deeper semantic abstraction and reasoning to identify commonalities.

#### Role of Aspect-Aware Cache

Table 2 shows the benefits of incorporating the aspect-aware cache into our Next Query Selection strategy (described in Section 3.3), which enables preventing redundant exploration within each aspect branch and thus encouraging more diverse search trajectories. From this, CoR with the aspect-aware cache consistently outperforms those without it, demonstrating its effectiveness in steering the retrieval process toward broader coverage and stronger overall performance.

#### Efficacy of Query Preference Optimization

To assess the contribution of reinforcing aspect-aware query optimizers with DPO, we conduct an ablation study isolating the DPO training. As shown in Table 3, integrating DPO consistently improves performance across diverse LLM-retriever configurations in both the reference and citation setups. Notably, although the preference pairs are constructed in the Reference (outgoing-links) setting using Recall as the reward signal, the gains transfer to other evaluation setups of Citation (incoming-links).

#### Analysis on Post-Order Aggregation

To verify whether our aggregation mechanism is responsible for performance improvements beyond those obtained from multi-aspect expansion, we conduct an analysis. As shown in Figure 5, CoR yields performance gains across successive retrieval rounds, with the gap over baselines widening as depth increases. This confirms the effectiveness of our post-order aggregation, which progressively attenuates weak signals from distant connections and thereby enhances robustness against noise in deeper rounds. By contrast, the baseline strategy (merging results from all branches at once) fails to adaptively penalize such signals, leading to steadily diminishing performance. However, improvements plateau beyond depth 3, which suggests diminishing returns, likely due to added noise with deeper expansions.

#### Diversity Analysis

Recall that CoR is designed to expand the search space iteratively across multiple aspects of the query paper, and we further analyze this by measuring the semantic coverage of retrieved candidates over ground-truth in the embedding space using the Convex Hull Volume Ratio (CHV Ratio), which compares coverage between two configurations, with the same set (see Appendix C.3 for details). As shown in Table 4, CoR consistently improves the diversity of semantic coverage among the retrieved documents: relative to the baseline A2A setup, it achieves a 14.98% gain in CHV Ratio, surpassing the 10.72% gain of the F2F setup. Moreover, when directly compared against F2F, CoR still provides an additional 6.52% improvement. These results highlight that beyond improving retrieval accuracy, the proposed CoR enables broader semantic exploration, which allows discovering relevant papers that would likely be missed under the vanilla retrieval strategies.

#### Generalization to Other Domains

To examine the generality of CoR beyond scientific paper retrieval, we further evaluate its performance on a different but challenging document-to-document retrieval task: patent-to-patent retrieval, which has substantially long queries (please see Appendix D for details on task design and implementation). As shown in Table 5, CoR delivers robust gains over both the domain-agnostic and domain-specific baselines, surpassing F2F retrieval by 2.01% and A2A retrieval by 6.96%. Importantly, these improvements are achieved without any training (i.e., using the off-the-shelf GPT-4o for query optimization), highlighting the versatility and broad applicability of CoR for long document-to-document retrieval.

#### Human Evaluation

To further assess the quality of retrieved results beyond the citation-based ground truth in SciFullBench, we conduct a human evaluation. A total of 15 participants evaluate the relevance of the Top-5 retrieved candidates for three methods (A2A, F2F, CoR) across 15 query papers, assigning one of four labels to each candidate (motivation-relevant, method-relevant, experiment-relevant, or irrelevant). We then compute per-query precision by treating any of the three aspect labels as relevant and the remaining label as irrelevant. As shown in Table 6, CoR achieves the highest precision, surpassing A2A and F2F by 3.34% and 10.84%, respectively, indicating that its improvements extend beyond citation-based metrics to human-perceived relevance. To ensure the reliability of human judgments, we measure inter-annotator agreement on it with Cohen’s Kappa coefficient (Cohen, 1960), obtaining a score of 0.43, which corresponds to moderate agreement and supports the reliability of our human evaluation. For further details, please refer to Appendix C.4.

## 5 Conclusion

In this work, we introduced Chain of Retrieval (in short, CoR), a novel framework for paper-to-paper retrieval that iteratively expands the search space via aspect-aware query optimization (reinforced with DPO training) and recursively merges results via post-order aggregation. For evaluation, we presented SciFullBench, a large-scale dataset for full-context scientific retrieval, and results show that CoR consistently outperforms the abstract-level and full-context baselines, even with off-the-shelf embedding models and for a patent retrieval task, highlighting its robustness and generality.

## Limitations

While our work introduces a novel retrieval approach that iteratively expands the search space via multi-aspect query optimization over the full context of scientific papers, it still has room for future work. First, an adaptive branch pruning mechanism could be further considered during the exploration phase to more dynamically guide the search results with the semantic alignment of individual papers with the root query, which would be an interesting direction for future work. Second, while our framework retrieves diverse and relevant papers, deeper exploration and repeated LLM inference introduce additional computational overhead. While we partially mitigate this with a lightweight selection mechanism (in place of expensive LLM verifiers), further optimizations on it would be a valuable direction, which we leave as future work.

## Ethics Statement

Although our Chain of Retrieval (CoR) framework improves retrieval performance over prior approaches, it can still retrieve irrelevant or misleading papers, which may propagate incorrect or harmful information to both human users and downstream AI models. To ensure the development of trustworthy automated systems, future work should incorporate robust verification or re-ranking mechanisms that can effectively filter irrelevant or potentially harmful documents from the retrieved set.
